tech-azure-apps.title: Azure developer & platform labs: App Service, Functions, AKS, SQL, Monitor, Bicep
tech-azure-apps.description: Hands-on Azure application platform programme: App Service, Functions, AKS, Azure SQL, Azure Monitor/KQL and ARM/Bicep - every lesson is a CLI lab, SQL/KQL exercise, ticket or console checklist. Tags 'AZ-104-level' / 'Azure AZ-204' are topic tags only, not official. All labs are simulated consoles (invented accounts, hosts and IDs) - nothing touches a real cloud. For real practice use each provider's free tier or a sandbox account, and switch on billing alerts/budgets before you start.

courses.title: Azure App Service: deploy, scale, slots

ticket.description: Since about 7 pm patients can't book appointments, error 503 on and off. Busy evening hour.

investigate.label: Autoscale run history
investigate.reveal: 18:55 scale in 4→1 (rule: CPU < 60% for 5 min). 19:02 scale out 1→2 (CPU > 80%)...

investigate.label: Metrics
investigate.reveal: Memory working set 98% on the single instance at 18:58; Http5xx spike.

investigate.label: SSL certificate
investigate.reveal: Valid till 2027-03.

investigate.label: Key Vault access
investigate.reveal: References resolved OK.

options: An aggressive scale-in rule left one instance that ran out of memory at peak

resolution: Manually scale out to 4 instances to restore service
Change autoscale: minimum 3, scale-in on CPU < 30% for 15 min
Add a memory-based scale-out rule
Enable health check path /healthz

courses.title: Azure Functions: triggers, bindings and plans

steps.title: Function app
steps.body: A function app needs a storage account (for triggers/state) and a hosting plan. Use Core Tools locally: `func init`, `func new`, `func start`, then `func azure functionapp publish`.

steps.title: Plans
steps.body: Consumption: scale to zero, pay per execution. Flex Consumption: faster scale, VNet. Premium: pre-warmed instances, VNet, no cold start. Dedicated: on an App Service plan.

steps.title: App Insights
steps.body: Turn on Application Insights from day one.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: Exactly one **trigger** per function (HTTP, Timer, Blob, Queue, Service Bus, Event Grid, Event Hubs, Cosmos DB...). Optional input/output **bindings** connect data declaratively.

steps.title: Timer
steps.body: CRON with seconds: `0 */5 * * * *` = every 5 minutes.

steps.title: Event Grid for blobs
steps.body: For high-scale blob events, the Event Grid-based blob trigger is faster than polling.

scenes.text: Lab results need doctor approval within 24 h, else escalate.

steps.title: Durable
steps.body: Orchestrator functions coordinate activity functions with state checkpointed in storage. Patterns: function chaining, fan-out/fan-in, async HTTP APIs, monitor, human interaction (wait for external event with timeout).

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: Orchestrator code must be deterministic - no DateTime.Now or random; use context APIs.

steps.title: Alternative
steps.body: Logic Apps for low-code workflows.

scenes.text: Some orders never get processed.
Imran finds the -poison queue.

steps.title: Poison messages
steps.body: Queue trigger retries a message up to maxDequeueCount (default 5), then moves it to `<queue>-poison`. Service Bus uses dead-letter queues.

steps.title: Alert
steps.body: Alert on poison/DLQ length > 0.

steps.title: Replay
steps.body: Fix the bug, then replay poison messages safely (idempotent handlers).

ticket.description: About 1 in 50 orders since Tuesday never get confirmation SMS. Customers calling.

investigate.label: Queue 'orders-poison'
investigate.reveal: 312 messages since Tuesday 11:00.

investigate.label: App Insights exceptions
investigate.reveal: KeyError 'pincode' - new mobile app version sends 'pinCode'.

investigate.label: Function scale
investigate.reveal: Normal.

investigate.label: SMS provider status
investigate.reveal: Operational.

options: A payload field rename makes the handler throw; after 5 retries messages go to poison

resolution: Hotfix handler to accept both pincode and pinCode with validation
Deploy and verify new messages succeed
Replay the 312 poison messages through an idempotent re-queue script
Add an alert on poison queue length
Agree a schema contract with the mobile team

closure.prompt: Write the resolution/closure note for the ticket
closure.model: Root cause: app v5.2 renamed 'pincode' to 'pinCode'; the function threw KeyError, after 5 dequeues messages moved to orders-poison (312). Fix: tolerant parsing deployed, poison messages replayed. Verification: 312 confirmations sent, poison queue 0. Prevention: alert + JSON schema contract tests.

tech-build-devices.title: How devices are built: phones, displays, batteries, PCBs & laptops
tech-build-devices.description: From chips to products: smartphone teardown and assembly lines, LCD/OLED/LTPO display fabs, lithium-ion cell manufacturing and safety, PCB fabrication and SMT lines, and laptop assembly with service tickets.

courses.title: How a smartphone is built
courses.summary: Inside a modern phone and its factory: SoC, memory, modem and RF, cameras, sensors, display, battery; mainboard SMT, sub-assemblies, final assembly, calibration and quality tests (drop, water, RF) — with an exploded 3D teardown.
outcomes: Identify phone components in an exploded view
Explain what the SoC integrates

scenes.text: Kavya's phone slipped into a lake; she wonders which parts the water could reach.

steps.title: Main parts
steps.body:
- **Display module** (cover glass, touch, OLED/LCD panel).
- **Mainboard** (often stacked 'sandwich' boards): **SoC** (CPU, GPU, NPU, ISP, modem on many chips), LPDDR RAM (often package-on-package), UFS storage, PMIC, RF front-end, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth.
- **Battery** (Li-ion pouch, ~4,000–5,500 mAh typical in many phones).
- **Cameras** (several modules with image sensors, lenses, OIS).
- **Speakers, vibration motor, antennas, sensors** (accelerometer, gyro, proximity, ambient light, fingerprint).
- **Frame and back cover**, gaskets/adhesives for water resistance.

steps.title: SoC
steps.body: A system-on-chip integrates CPU cores, GPU, neural processor, image signal processor, memory controllers and often the cellular modem — one die doing what used to be a whole motherboard.

steps.title: Water resistance
steps.body: IP ratings (IEC 60529): first digit dust (6 = dust-tight), second water (7 = immersion up to 1 m for 30 min; 8 = beyond, per the maker's stated conditions). Seals age — water resistance is not permanent.

steps.title: Flow
steps.body: SMT mainboard → board test (ICT/FCT, RF calibration) → sub-assemblies (display module, camera modules) → final assembly in the frame → software flashing → functional test (touch, display, cameras, audio, sensors) → RF/antenna test in shielded boxes → water-resistance (air-leak) test → cosmetic inspection → packing.

courses.title: Display technology & manufacturing: LCD, OLED, LTPO
courses.summary: How screens work and are made: TFT backplanes (a-Si, LTPS, oxide/IGZO, LTPO), LCD with backlights, OLED stacks and fine-metal-mask evaporation, encapsulation, mini/micro-LED, touch and lamination — plus refresh rates and power.

scenes.text: Ravi notices that black areas on his OLED phone look truly black, but his LCD laptop glows grey in the dark.
LCDs filter a backlight; OLED pixels emit their own light and can switch fully off.

steps.title: LCD
steps.body: Backlight (LEDs + light guide) → polariser → TFT array → liquid crystal → colour filter → polariser. Each pixel twists light to pass or block it. Mature, cheap, bright; blacks limited by leakage; mini-LED backlights with local dimming improve contrast.

steps.title: OLED
steps.body: Each subpixel is an organic light-emitting diode on a TFT backplane, sealed by thin-film encapsulation (oxygen/moisture kill organics). True blacks, thin, flexible/foldable; challenges: burn-in (differential ageing), cost, blue lifetime.

steps.title: Backplanes
steps.body:
- **a-Si TFT**: cheap, low mobility (large LCD TVs).
- **LTPS**: high mobility (phones).
- **Oxide (IGZO)**: low leakage, good for large panels and low refresh.
- **LTPO**: LTPS + oxide combination enabling variable refresh down to ~1 Hz for always-on displays.

steps.title: Micro-LED
steps.body: Inorganic micro-scale LEDs per pixel promise brightness and lifetime, but mass transfer of millions of tiny LEDs is still a manufacturing challenge.

scenes.text: Phone OLEDs are made on large glass or polyimide 'mother' substrates in display fabs, then cut into panels.

steps.title: Key steps
steps.body: Backplane TFT (litho, deposition, etch — like a chip fab but on big glass) → OLED evaporation through **fine metal masks** (FMM) for RGB subpixels in vacuum → cathode → **thin-film encapsulation** → touch layer → cut into panels → polariser/cover lamination → module (driver IC bonding, flex) → test/aging.

steps.title: Flexible OLED
steps.body: Built on polyimide on a glass carrier; later laser lift-off releases the flexible panel.

courses.title: Battery chemistry & cell manufacturing
courses.summary: Lithium-ion from atoms to packs: cathodes (LCO, NMC, NCA, LFP), graphite/silicon anodes, electrolyte, separator; electrode coating, calendering, winding/stacking, filling, formation and ageing; C-rates, Wh, safety and travel rules.
outcomes: Explain how a Li-ion cell stores energy
Compare cathode chemistries and their uses
Order the cell manufacturing process
Compute Wh, C-rate, energy density and airline limits

scenes.text: In a Li-ion cell, lithium ions rock back and forth between two electrodes; electrons take the outside path through your phone.
Abuse — puncture, overcharge, overheating — can trigger thermal runaway.

steps.title: Parts
steps.body:
- **Cathode** (positive): lithium metal oxide or phosphate on aluminium foil.
- **Anode** (negative): graphite (sometimes with silicon) on copper foil.
- **Separator**: porous polymer that blocks electrons, passes ions.
- **Electrolyte**: lithium salt (e.g. LiPF₆) in organic solvents.
Charging pushes Li⁺ into the graphite; discharging returns it to the cathode.

steps.title: Chemistries
steps.body:
- **LCO**: high energy density; phones/laptops (older/common in small cells).
- **NMC / NCA**: high energy; EVs, power tools.
- **LFP**: lower energy density but very safe, long cycle life, no cobalt/nickel — popular for EVs and storage.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Never charge swollen batteries; don't puncture; use certified chargers. Thermal runaway can spread cell to cell.

steps.title: SEI
steps.body: The solid-electrolyte interphase forms on the anode during first charges (formation); it protects the cell but consumes some lithium.

activity.prompt: Explore a pouch cell stack in 3D. Tap each layer.

objects.label: Aluminium foil (cathode current collector)
objects.info: Carries electrons from the cathode coating.

objects.label: Cathode coating
objects.info: e.g. LCO, NMC or LFP particles with binder and carbon.

objects.label: Separator
objects.info: Porous polymer: ions pass, electrons don't.

objects.label: Copper foil (anode current collector)
objects.info: Copper is used because aluminium alloys with lithium at anode potentials.

scenes.text: A cell factory has three zones: electrodes, cell assembly, and formation/ageing.
Order the steps.

steps.title: Why dry rooms
steps.body: Electrolyte reacts with water to form HF; cell assembly happens in dry rooms with very low dew points.

steps.title: Formation
steps.body: Slow first charge cycles build the SEI; ageing over days screens out cells with self-discharge (micro-shorts).

Insert into can/pouch and weld tabs

courses.title: How data centres are built: power, cooling & PUE
courses.summary: Data-centre engineering: site, utility feeds, transformers, generators, UPS and batteries, PDUs, redundancy tiers (N, N+1, 2N), hot/cold-aisle containment, CRAH/chillers, free cooling, liquid cooling for AI racks, PUE and WUE numericals.
outcomes: Trace the power path from grid to server
Compute PUE, UPS runtime and cooling load
Explain redundancy levels and containment
Run a cooling-incident scenario

scenes.text: A data hall holds hundreds of racks; behind the walls sit transformers, UPS rooms, batteries, generators and chillers.
Every watt used by servers needs extra energy to deliver and cool it.

steps.title: Power path
steps.body: Utility (HV) → substation/transformers → main switchgear → UPS (batteries/flywheels) → PDUs/busways → rack PDUs → server PSUs. Diesel (or other) generators start within seconds on utility failure; the UPS bridges the gap.

steps.title: Cooling
steps.body: Hot/cold aisle layout with **containment**; CRAH/CRAC units with chilled water or DX; **free cooling** (economisers) when outside air is cool; **liquid cooling** (direct-to-chip cold plates, rear-door heat exchangers, immersion) for dense AI racks (often 30–100+ kW per rack).

steps.title: Redundancy
steps.body: N = just enough; **N+1** = one spare; **2N** = fully duplicated paths (A/B). Tier classifications describe availability design levels.

steps.title: PUE
steps.body: Power Usage Effectiveness = total facility power ÷ IT power. 1.0 is ideal; modern efficient sites report ~1.1–1.4.

activity.prompt: Explore the data centre: tour from power room to data hall.

tour.text: Data hall with contained cold aisles.

scenes.text: IT load 1,600 kW; total facility 2,400 kW.
Compute PUE.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: PUE = 2400/1600 = **1.5**. Overhead (cooling, losses, lighting) = 800 kW.

steps.title: Improvement
steps.body: If cooling upgrades cut overhead to 400 kW: PUE = 2000/1600 = 1.25, saving 400 kW → ~3.5 GWh per year (400 kW × 8,760 h).

steps.title: WUE
steps.body: Water Usage Effectiveness = annual water (litres) ÷ IT energy (kWh) — important where water is scarce.

steps.title: UPS
steps.body: Runtime = 40 × 0.95 / 200 h = 0.19 h = **11.4 min** — enough for generators to start and sync (typically well under a minute).

steps.title: Cooling
steps.body: 12 kW rack → 12 × 3,412 = 40,944 BTU/h ≈ 12/3.517 ≈ 3.4 tons of refrigeration.

steps.title: Battery ageing
steps.body: Capacity falls with age and temperature; test batteries regularly.

rounds.q: A PC powers on, fans spin, but there's no display. Walk me through it.
rounds.model: First I'd confirm the monitor is on the right input and the cable is on the GPU. Then check debug LEDs or beep codes to see the failing stage. If DRAM, reseat RAM and try one stick in the recommended slot; if VGA, reseat the GPU and power cables. I'd clear CMOS and, if needed, strip to a minimal configuration and swap known-good parts one at a time, then document the root cause.
followups: What if the CPU LED stays on with a brand-new CPU?

rounds.q: How do you size a power supply for a new build?
rounds.model: Add up typical power of CPU, GPU and the rest, then add 20–40% headroom for transients and efficiency; for example 385 W load leads to a quality 550–650 W unit. Check it has the right CPU EPS and GPU connectors and a good efficiency rating.
followups: Why not buy a 1,500 W PSU for everything?

rounds.q: A user's laptop overheats and shuts down on video calls. What do you check?
rounds.model: I'd check logs for thermal shutdowns, monitor temperatures and fan speed under load, then inspect the heatsink for dust and the thermal paste. After cleaning and re-pasting and updating BIOS/EC firmware, I'd run a stress test to verify temperatures stay safe before closing the ticket.
followups: How do you handle it if the laptop is under warranty?

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you handled an upset user.
rounds.model: Use STAR: describe the situation, listen and acknowledge, set clear expectations and updates, resolve or escalate, and follow up to confirm satisfaction.

rounds.q: What is ESD and how do you prevent damage?
rounds.model: ESD is a sudden discharge of static electricity that can damage components. I ground myself with a wrist strap or by touching grounded metal, work on an ESD mat, keep parts in anti-static bags and handle boards by the edges.

tips: Structure: context → approach → numbers → trade-offs → how you'd verify.

rounds.q: Explain PUE and calculate it for 1.6 MW IT and 2.4 MW total.
rounds.model: PUE is total facility power divided by IT power. Here 2.4 / 1.6 = 1.5, meaning 0.8 MW goes to overhead such as cooling and electrical losses. Lower is better; efficient sites are around 1.1–1.4.

rounds.q: A server reports 'PSU redundancy lost'. What do you do?
rounds.model: I'd check the BMC event log and sensors to see which PSU failed and why. If AC was lost, I'd check the cord and the PDU/breaker on that feed — if multiple servers show it, the PDU or feed is suspect. If the PSU itself failed, I'd hot-swap it under a change ticket and verify redundancy is restored.
followups: What if many servers in the rack show the same alert?

rounds.q: What does N+1 vs 2N mean?
rounds.model: N is the capacity needed. N+1 adds one spare unit so one failure doesn't cause loss. 2N duplicates the whole system — for example separate A and B power paths — so an entire path can fail or be maintained without impact.

rounds.q: Inlet temperatures in an aisle are rising. Steps?
rounds.model: Check the cooling units and chilled-water supply for that zone, follow the runbook to restart or fail over, verify containment doors and blanking panels are in place, escalate as an incident if SLAs are at risk, and then investigate root cause and N+1 margin.

rounds.q: How do you rack a heavy server safely?
rounds.model: Follow the change ticket and rack elevation, deploy stabilisers, install rails, use a two-person lift or lift aid, secure the server, connect PSUs to A and B PDUs, cable and label per the plan, power on, verify BMC health and update the CMDB.

steps.title: Model types
steps.body:
- **Wireframe:** edges only, no faces.
- **Surface:** faces without volume (good for curved skins).
- **Solid:** closed volume with mass properties — what you need for manufacturing and BIM quantities. **Note:** CAD software (AutoCAD, SolidWorks, Fusion, Revit or similar) must be installed separately on your computer; VidyaVerse does not run it. Labs give exact steps and values so you can practise there and check yourself here.

steps.title: Exact steps (any solid modeller)
steps.body:
1. Sketch on the top plane: rectangle 100 × 60, corner at origin.
2. Extrude 20 mm.
3. Sketch a circle Ø20 at (50,30) on the top face; Extruded Cut → Through All.
4. Mass properties: volume expected = 100×60×20 − π×10²×20 = 120,000 − 6,283.19 = **113,716.81 mm³**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Open sketch profile: extrusion fails because the profile is not closed.
- Sketching the circle on the wrong plane.

steps.title: Feature types
steps.body:
- **Extrude:** straight along a vector.
- **Revolve:** profile around an axis.
- **Sweep:** profile along a path.
- **Loft:** blends between two or more profiles.

steps.title: Worked example · revolve

courses.title: Parametric Modelling: Sketch Constraints, Parameters, SolidWorks & Fusion Concepts
courses.summary: Fully-defined sketches, dimensional relations, named parameters, feature trees and design tables — concepts shared by SolidWorks, Fusion and similar tools. Software must be installed separately.
outcomes: Explain under-, fully- and over-defined sketches
Drive models with named parameters and equations
Plan a robust feature order

scenes.text: Neha's model breaks when she changes one dimension.
Constraints capture design intent.

steps.title: Constraints and states
steps.body: Geometric relations: horizontal, vertical, coincident, tangent, concentric, parallel, perpendicular, equal, symmetric. Dimensions add size. In SolidWorks, an **under-defined** sketch shows blue geometry, **fully defined** black, **over-defined** red. Fusion uses blue (under) and black (fully constrained) similarly. **Note:** CAD software (AutoCAD, SolidWorks, Fusion, Revit or similar) must be installed separately on your computer; VidyaVerse does not run it. Labs give exact steps and values so you can practise there and check yourself here.

steps.title: Degrees of freedom
steps.body: A free line in 2D has 4 DOF (two endpoints × x,y). Horizontal removes 1, a length dimension 1, fixing one end 2 → fully defined: 4−1−1−2=0.

steps.title: Rectangle
steps.body: Four free lines have 16 DOF. Four coincident corner joins remove 8, leaving 8. Horizontal/vertical relations on the four sides remove 4 more, leaving 4 (corner position x,y plus width and height). Fixing one corner at the origin removes 2, so just 2 dimensions (width, height) fully define it.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Adding a dimension that already follows from constraints creates red over-definition; delete the redundant one.

activity.prompt: A free rectangle has 8 DOF after joins and horizontal/vertical relations reduce it to 4 (position 2 + size 2). Dimensions needed to fully define it (with origin corner fixed)?

steps.title: Parameters
steps.body: Name dimensions (`width`, `thk`). Write equations: `hole_x = width/2`. In Fusion use Modify → Change Parameters (user parameters like `d1 = 100 mm`). In SolidWorks use Tools → Equations.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: width = 100, hole_dia = width/10 = 10, hole_pitch = width/2 = 50. Change width to 140 → hole_dia 14, pitch 70 automatically.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: At width 140 the hole at pitch 70 sits at mid-width, 70 from each edge.

steps.title: Naming
steps.body: Use clear names: `plate_width`, `wall_thk`; never leave d1, d2 in complex models.

courses.summary: BIM concepts, levels and grids, walls, floors, stairs, families, schedules and sheets — described as steps for Revit-style tools. Software must be installed separately.
outcomes: Explain BIM, LOD and IFC

scenes.text: Studio project: a 3-storey block, floor-to-floor 3000 mm.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: BIM idea
steps.body: Building Information Modelling is one coordinated model from which plans, sections, schedules and quantities are views. Elements carry data (type, material, fire rating). Open exchange format: **IFC**. Standards: **ISO 19650** for information management. **Note:** CAD software (AutoCAD, SolidWorks, Fusion, Revit or similar) must be installed separately on your computer; VidyaVerse does not run it. Labs give exact steps and values so you can practise there and check yourself here.

steps.title: Exact steps
steps.body:
1. Architecture template (metric). In an elevation view set Level 1 = 0, Level 2 = 3000, Level 3 = 6000.
2. Grid: `GR` → draw A–C at 6000 spacing in X; 1–3 at 5000 in Y.
3. Wall: Architecture → Wall, type Generic 230 (or brick 230), Base Level 1, Top Level 2, location line Wall Centerline.
4. Check in 3D: wall height 3000.

steps.title: Calculation
steps.body: Slab 150 → clear height = 3000 − 150 = 2850 mm (before finishes).

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Setting an 'unconnected height' of 3000 instead of constraining to levels, so moving a level does not move the wall.

scenes.text: Level 1 to 2 is 3000 mm.

steps.title: Stair design
steps.body: Number of risers = floor-to-floor ÷ riser height. Treads = risers − 1 in a straight flight. Going = treads × tread depth.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: Riser 150: 3000/150 = 20 risers; 19 treads; tread 250 → going 4750 mm. Check with the local rule (NBC India residential: riser ≤ 190, tread ≥ 250, confirm current edition).

steps.title: Try 187.5
steps.body: 3000/16 = 187.5 mm riser, 15 treads × 250 = 3750 going.

steps.title: Revit
steps.body: Architecture → Stair → By Component; Desired Number of Risers set from level height automatically.

scenes.text: A 6.0 m wall must fit an A3 sheet.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: ISO A series
steps.body: A0 = 841 × 1189 mm (1 m²), each next size halves: A1 594×841, A2 420×594, A3 297×420, A4 210×297. Preferred reduction scales: 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, 1:20, 1:50, 1:100, 1:200; enlargement 2:1, 5:1. **Note:** CAD software (AutoCAD, SolidWorks, Fusion, Revit or similar) must be installed separately on your computer; VidyaVerse does not run it. Labs give exact steps and values so you can practise there and check yourself here.

steps.title: Fit
steps.body: 6000 mm at 1:20 = 300 mm — too long for A3's 297 usable. 1:50 → 120 mm fits.

steps.title: Scale conversion
steps.body: At 1:50, 25 mm on paper = 1250 mm real.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Quoting scale on a drawing that has been 'fit to page' printed; use a graphic scale bar when sharing PDFs.

scenes.text: Indian and ISO practice uses first angle; US practice uses third.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: **First angle** (used in India, ISO): object between observer and plane — front view top-left; top view is *below* the front view; left view is on the *right*. **Third angle** (US, ASME): plane between observer and object — top view above front; right view on the right. Symbol: truncated cone drawn in the title block.

steps.title: Memory
steps.body: First angle: 'what you see is placed on the opposite side'.

steps.title: Always state
steps.body: Mention the projection symbol in the title block to avoid factory errors.

steps.title: Line types
steps.body: Thick continuous: visible outlines. Thin continuous: dimensions, hatching. Dashed: hidden edges. Chain thin: centre lines. Chain thick at ends: cutting plane. Hatching at 45° with uniform spacing.

steps.title: Section types
steps.body: Full, half, offset, revolved, removed, broken-out. Webs, ribs and shafts are normally not hatched when cut longitudinally.

steps.title: Dimensioning rules
steps.body: Place dimensions outside views, avoid duplicate dimensions, give size and location, use a consistent unit (mm) and no unit symbol on the drawing.

steps.title: Mistake

courses.summary: Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing from datums to position tolerance with MMC and bonus tolerance, with numerical exercises. Independent study companion; always follow your organisation's current standard (ASME Y14.5 or ISO GPS).
outcomes: Read a feature control frame

lessons.title: Lab: Read a feature control frame

scenes.text: A drawing says ⌖ Ø0.2 Ⓜ | A | B. What does it demand?
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Feature control frame
steps.body: Left to right: symbol (characteristic), tolerance zone (Ø if cylindrical), value, modifier (Ⓜ MMC, Ⓛ LMC), then datum references in priority order. Datum A is primary (constrains 3 DOF if a plane), B secondary, C tertiary.

steps.title: Characteristic families
steps.body: Form (flatness, straightness, circularity, cylindricity — no datums), orientation (perpendicularity, parallelism, angularity), location (position, concentricity, symmetry), runout (circular, total), profile (line, surface).

steps.title: Reading
steps.body: ⌖ Ø0.2 | A | B: hole axis must lie within a cylinder of Ø0.2 whose axis is at true position relative to datums A then B.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Adding datum references to form tolerances such as flatness; these never take datums.

lessons.title: Lab: Position tolerance and MMC bonus

scenes.text: A hole Ø10.0–10.2 has position Ø0.1 at MMC.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: MMC
steps.body: Maximum Material Condition: hole at its smallest size (Ø10.0), shaft at largest. With Ⓜ the position tolerance grows by the departure from MMC (bonus).

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: Hole Ø10.0–10.2, position Ø0.1 Ⓜ. Actual size 10.15 → bonus = 10.15 − 10.0 = 0.15 → total allowed position Ø0.25. At 10.2: bonus 0.2 → Ø0.3 total.

steps.title: Shaft case
steps.body: Pin Ø9.8–9.9, MMC = 9.9. Actual 9.85 → bonus 0.05.

steps.title: Why
steps.body: Bigger clearance means more position freedom while still assembling.

steps.body: Primary datum plane contacts 3 points (stops 3 DOF), secondary plane 2 points (2 DOF), tertiary 1 point (1 DOF) = 6 DOF constrained.

steps.title: Choosing
steps.body: Choose A = mounting face (largest, flat), B = long edge, C = short edge. Hole positions then reference A|B|C.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Selecting a rough, curved or non-functional feature as a datum.

steps.title: Inspection
steps.body: The datum features are placed on a CMM or fixture in the same A-B-C order.

Check: worst case both at MMC with Ø0.2 error: 7.8+0.2 = 8.0 → fits.

steps.body: If a hole measures 8.1 the allowed zone is 0.2 + 0.1 = Ø0.3.

tech-cad-autocad.title: AutoCAD 2D from Zero
tech-cad-autocad.description: Learn AutoCAD 2D from first launch to a plotted 2BHK plan. CAD software must be installed separately (AutoCAD or any CAD that uses the same commands); labs give exact keystrokes and dimensions so you can practise in your own software.

courses.title: AutoCAD 2D · Interface, Units & Your First Drawing
courses.summary: Start from zero: workspace, the command line, units, coordinate entry, object snaps and a first dimensioned plate. Needs AutoCAD installed separately; every lab lists exact keystrokes.
outcomes: Set drawing units and a metric template
Enter points with absolute, relative and polar coordinates
Use object snaps, ortho and polar tracking
Draw a simple plate with a hole to exact dimensions

lessons.title: Lab: Set units and a template

story.title: Anil opens AutoCAD for the first time

scenes.text: Anil sees a black screen, a ribbon and a command line and does not know where to begin.
His studio asks for millimetres, so every wall must be drawn 1 unit = 1 mm.

steps.title: The screen
steps.body: Key areas: **Application menu**, **Ribbon**, **Drawing area** (model space), **Command line** (bottom), **Status bar** (snap, grid, ortho, polar, osnap toggles) and **ViewCube/Navigation bar**. The command line is the heart of AutoCAD: type a command name or alias, then press **Enter** or **Space**, and answer the prompts. **Note:** AutoCAD (or a compatible 2D CAD program using the same command names) must be installed separately on your own computer; VidyaVerse does not run CAD. These labs give the exact keystrokes and values so you can follow them in your own software and then check yourself here.

steps.title: Units
steps.body: Type **UNITS** and Enter. Set Type = Decimal, Precision = 0, and *Insertion scale* (units to scale inserted content) = Millimeters. AutoCAD units are unitless; *you* decide 1 unit = 1 mm. Architects in India usually draw in mm (or metres with 0.00 precision); mixing both inside one drawing is the commonest beginner error.

steps.title: Limits and zoom
steps.body: Modern AutoCAD needs no limits; use `ZOOM` then `E` (Extents) whenever you cannot see your work.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing a 3 m wall as `3` instead of `3000` in a mm drawing.
- Forgetting to press Esc twice to cancel a command before starting another.
- Saving only as .dwg and never making a template.

activity.prompt: Arrange the steps to prepare a millimetre template
items: Type UNITS and press Enter
Choose Decimal type, precision 0
Set insertion scale to Millimeters
Click OK
Type SAVEAS and choose the .dwt template type

quiz.q: Which command opens the drawing units dialog?
quiz.why: UNITS controls type, precision, angle format and insertion scale.

quiz.q: In a mm drawing, a 3 m wall is drawn with length
quiz.why: 1 drawing unit = 1 mm, so 3 m = 3000 units.

quiz.q: How do you finish or repeat a command quickly?
quiz.why: Enter/Space accept input; pressing Enter on an empty prompt repeats the last command.

lessons.title: Lab: Absolute, relative and polar coordinates

scenes.text: Meera must draw a triangle without a mouse, only coordinates.
She learns three ways to tell AutoCAD where a point is.

steps.title: Three input styles
steps.body:
- **Absolute:** `x,y` measured from the origin (0,0), e.g. `100,50`.
- **Relative:** `@dx,dy` measured from the last point, e.g. `@200,0`.
- **Polar:** `@distance<angle`, angle measured counter-clockwise from the +X axis (east = 0°, north = 90°), e.g. `@100<60`.
Turn **Dynamic Input** (F12) off while you learn so that you type the symbols yourself.

steps.title: Worked example · triangle
steps.body:
Command: `LINE`
- Specify first point: `0,0`
- Next point: `@100<0` → (100, 0)
- Next point: `@100<120` → x = 100 + 100cos120° = 50, y = 100sin120° ≈ 86.60
- Next point: `C` (Close) returns to (0,0).
The triangle is equilateral with side 100.

steps.title: Direct distance entry
steps.body: With Ortho on (F8), point the cursor east and type `500` Enter: a 500-long horizontal line. Fast, but only for horizontal/vertical lines.

activity.prompt: LINE starts at 0,0 and the next point is entered as @5000<30. What is the Y coordinate of the end point (mm)?

quiz.q: In the polar entry @50<90 the line goes
quiz.why: 90° is measured counter-clockwise from east, so it points up.
@ makes the entered values relative to the previous point.

lessons.title: Lab: Object snaps, ortho and polar tracking

scenes.text: Ravi's lines look joined but have 0.3 mm gaps — the drawing fails a clash check.
Object snaps remove this guesswork.

steps.title: Why snaps
steps.body: Clicking visually near a corner is never exact. **Object snap (F3)** locks the cursor to Endpoint, Midpoint, Centre, Intersection, Perpendicular, Tangent, Nearest and more. Right-click the OSNAP status-bar button → Object Snap Settings to tick the ones you want (Endpoint, Midpoint, Centre, Intersection are a good default). Do not tick everything — the cursor will jump around.

steps.title: Ortho, polar, tracking
steps.body: **Ortho (F8)** forces 0/90°. **Polar tracking (F10)** shows alignment at set increments (e.g. 15° or 45°). **Object snap tracking (F11)** lets you align to a point you hover over without clicking. Ortho and polar are mutually exclusive.

steps.title: Snap to a midpoint
steps.body: Hover the top edge of a rectangle until the green triangle (Midpoint marker) appears, then click.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Turning on polar and ortho together expecting both.
- Using the *Nearest* snap and thinking the point is a corner.

Ortho allows only horizontal and vertical.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone · 100 × 60 plate with a Ø20 hole

scenes.text: A workshop wants a 100 × 60 mm plate with a Ø20 hole centred.
You will draw it exactly and verify the numbers.

steps.title: Exact steps
steps.body:
1. `RECTANG` (REC) Enter. First corner `0,0`. Other corner `@100,60`.
2. `CIRCLE` (C). Centre: `50,30`. Diameter: type `D` Enter then `20`.
3. `ZOOM` Enter `E` Enter to see everything.
4. Type `LIST`, select the circle: radius should read 10.0000 and area 314.1593.
5. Save the file as `plate-100x60.dwg`.

steps.title: Check by calculation
steps.body: Circle area = π r² = 3.14159 × 10² = 314.16 mm². Plate area = 100 × 60 = 6000 mm². Net area = 6000 − 314.16 = 5685.84 mm².

steps.title: Self-check
steps.body: Hover the circle centre: it should snap to the rectangle midpoint intersection if you draw diagonals temporarily. Erase them afterwards.

lessons.title: Lab: Offset, Trim and Extend a wall plan

scenes.text: Sunita has a 6000 × 4000 room outline and needs 230 mm thick walls.

steps.title: OFFSET (O)
steps.body: Creates a parallel copy at a set distance. Prompt: *Specify offset distance* → type the value; *Select object*; *click the side* to offset. Works on lines, circles, arcs and polylines.

steps.title: TRIM (TR) and EXTEND (EX)
steps.body: TRIM: press Enter at *Select objects* to select all as cutting edges, then click the part to remove. Hold **Shift** to extend instead. EXTEND is the reverse and Shift trims.

steps.title: Exact steps
steps.body:
1. `REC` `0,0` then `@6000,4000`.
2. `X` (explode) the rectangle so it is four lines (or use a polyline offset).
3. `O` Enter `230` Enter, select the rectangle, click outside → outer wall line.
4. Enter `O` `230` again and click inside → inner wall line.
Outer size = 6460 × 4460; inner = 5540 × 3540.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Offsetting a rectangle drawn as a polyline: it moves as one piece (good), but exploding first gives four lines (bad).
- Trim 'edge' options: selecting nothing as cutting edges uses *all* objects, usually what you want.

scenes.text: Rahul must place two beds mirrored about a centre line.

steps.title: The five transform commands
steps.body:
- `MOVE` (M): base point, then destination.
- `COPY` (CO): same, repeats until Enter.
- `ROTATE` (RO): base point, angle (positive = counter-clockwise); `R` Reference option.
- `SCALE` (SC): base point, factor; factor 0.5 halves.
- `MIRROR` (MI): two points define the mirror line; answer `N` to keep the original.

steps.title: Exact steps
steps.body:
1. Draw a bed 2000 × 1500 with `REC`.
2. `CO`, select, base point = a corner, then `@3000,0` to copy 3000 right.
3. `RO`, select the copy, base = its corner, type `90`.
4. `SC` to convert a drawing drawn in metres to mm: base 0,0, factor `1000`.

steps.title: Why base points
steps.body: Pick a base point you can later snap to (a corner or midpoint). The object then lands exactly where you expect.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Rotating by typing 270 when you meant −90 is the same, but mixing up clockwise with counter-clockwise rotates the wrong way.

steps.title: FILLET (F) and CHAMFER (CHA)
steps.body: `F` then `R` then radius, then pick two lines. Radius 0 makes sharp corners (also a quick way to close two lines). `CHA` then `D` sets two distances; chamfer cuts the corner with a straight bevel.

steps.title: Exact steps
steps.body:
1. `C` centre `0,0`, diameter `160`.
2. `C` again diameter `80` (centre bore).
3. `C` diameter `120` – this is the pitch circle; change it to a construction layer later.
4. Draw one bolt hole: `C` centre `60,0` diameter `14`.
5. `ARRAYPOLAR`, select the hole, centre `0,0`, items `6`, angle `360`.
6. Check: neighbouring holes are 60° apart; centre-to-centre distance = 2×60×sin(30°) = 60 mm.

steps.title: LAYER (LA)
steps.body: Open the Layer Properties Manager: New layer, name, colour, linetype, lineweight. Layers organise objects; use **ByLayer** colour/linetype/lineweight, never override per object. Layer 0 is special (blocks are made on 0).

steps.title: A typical set

- A-WALL (white/black, continuous, 0.50 mm)

steps.title: Standards
steps.body: Indian offices often follow their own layer standards; international ones commonly follow AIA/ISO 13567 naming. Pick one and keep to it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Making a layer and forgetting to set it Current before drawing.
- Freezing the current layer (not allowed) vs turning it off.
- Using colours that are invisible on a black background when plotting black.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: Model text height = paper text height × plot scale denominator. For 1:100 and 2.5 mm paper text: 2.5 × 100 = 250 mm model text height. At 1:50: 125 mm. At 1:20: 50 mm.

steps.title: Exact steps
steps.body:
1. `ST` (STYLE) → New 'A-NOTE', font Arial or simplex, height 0 (so you choose each time).
2. `MT` (MTEXT) → drag a box → set height to 250 → type text → Ctrl+Enter or OK.
3. For single line: `DT`, justify `M` (Middle), height 250.

steps.title: Annotative objects
steps.body: Annotative text/dimensions automatically scale to the viewport annotation scale, avoiding manual maths. Still know the maths for exams and older drawings.

steps.title: Another case
steps.body: A detail at 1:5 needs 3.5 mm notes: 3.5 × 5 = 17.5 mm model height.

steps.title: DIMSTYLE
steps.body: `D` opens Dimension Style Manager. Set Text height 2.5 (paper), Arrow size 2.5, Extension offset 1.5, Primary units Decimal precision 0, and **Use overall scale of** (DIMSCALE) = plot denominator (100 for 1:100) if not annotative. Then `DLI` (DIMLINEAR), `DAL` (aligned), `DRA` radius, `DDI` diameter, `DCO` continued, `DBA` baseline.

steps.title: HATCH (H)
steps.body: Pick internal point or select objects, choose pattern (ANSI31, AR-CONC, AR-BRSTD…), set scale so lines are readable (e.g. 1 in drawing units may need 50–200 for mm drawings), angle 0. Hatch on its own layer (A-HATCH).

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. `D` → Modify the Standard style → Fit tab → Use overall scale 100.
2. `DLI` → snap to two corners → drag → click.
3. `DCO` for chain dimensions after the first one.
4. `H` → pick a closed room → pattern ANSI31 scale 50.

steps.title: Don't
steps.body: Never type over a dimension value with text: it breaks associativity and creates wrong numbers.

steps.title: BLOCK (B), INSERT (I), WBLOCK
steps.body: `B`: name, base point, select objects. The block lives inside this drawing only. `W` (WBLOCK) writes it to a separate .dwg so any drawing can insert it. Blocks drawn on layer 0 with ByLayer properties take on the layer where they are inserted. Redefining a block updates all copies.

steps.title: Exact steps
steps.body:
1. On layer 0 draw a door: leaf `@900<90` from `0,0`, arc with start `900,0`.
2. `B` Enter, name `D900`, base point = hinge `0,0`, select the geometry, Delete after creation off → OK.
3. `I` → choose D900, scale 1, rotation 0 → click in a wall opening.
4. To flip use `MIRROR` or negative X scale on insert.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Exploding blocks (loses the one-change-updates-all benefit).
- Choosing base point = default 0,0 far from the object.
- Making blocks on coloured layers.

steps.title: Polyline (PL)
steps.body: One connected object of lines and arcs: `PL`, click points, `C` to close. `PEDIT` `J` joins lines into a polyline. Polylines can have width. `REC` and `POL` create closed polylines.

steps.title: AREA (AA)
steps.body: `AREA` then `O` (Object) and pick the polyline: area and perimeter are printed on the command line. Or `A` (Add area) with point clicks.

steps.title: Units
steps.body: In a mm drawing, AREA prints mm². Divide by 1,000,000 to get m².

steps.title: Model space vs paper space
steps.body: Model space holds the real-size drawing. Layout tabs are sheets of paper. A **viewport (MVIEW)** is a window onto the model; its scale is set to the plot scale (e.g. 1:100). Title block, notes and scale text live in the layout at 1:1.

steps.title: Exact steps
steps.body:
1. Click the Layout1 tab → right-click → Page Setup → printer *DWG To PDF*, paper A3 (420 × 297 mm), plot area Layout, scale 1:1.
2. `MV` (MVIEW) → rectangle on sheet.
3. Double-click inside the viewport, type `ZOOM` then `1/100XP`.
4. Double-click outside to return to paper space; lock the viewport (select it → Display Locked: Yes).
5. `PLOT` (Ctrl+P) → OK → save PDF.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Plotting at 'Fit to paper' (the scale is wrong).
- Zooming after the viewport is set but before locking it.
