tech-cloud-aws-gcp.title: AWS and Google Cloud essentials
tech-cloud-aws-gcp.description: Independent practice material for AWS Cloud Practitioner and Google Cloud Associate Cloud Engineer preparation, plus a Rosetta stone that maps Azure, AWS and Google Cloud services side by side. Not affiliated with or endorsed by any provider.

courses.title: AWS Cloud Practitioner essentials
courses.summary: Cloud concepts, global infrastructure, security and IAM, core services, and billing, pricing and support on AWS — explained from zero with scenario questions. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can explain AWS global infrastructure, the Well-Architected pillars and migration strategies
Learners can apply the shared responsibility model and IAM best practices
Learners can choose compute, storage, database and networking services for common scenarios
Learners can compare pricing models, cost tools and support plans

lessons.title: Cloud concepts and AWS global infrastructure

scenes.text: Two friends in Indore, Aman and Sophia, started an app streaming local cricket leagues. Match days brought 50 times the normal traffic.
They ran it on AWS in the Mumbai Region across multiple Availability Zones, and used a content delivery network so viewers in small towns got smooth video from nearby edge locations.
A mentor reviewed their design against the AWS Well-Architected Framework. 'Your reliability is good,' she said, 'but your cost optimisation is weak — servers run all night with no matches.'

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline (the exam code and domains are updated from time to time). AWS service names and features change — verify details in official documentation.

steps.title: Global infrastructure
steps.body:
- **Region:** a physical location in the world with multiple Availability Zones (e.g. Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Hyderabad)). Choose by compliance/data residency, latency to users, service availability and price.
- **Availability Zone (AZ):** one or more discrete data centres with redundant power and networking in a Region. Regions typically have three or more AZs. Deploy across AZs for high availability.
- **Edge locations:** points of presence for Amazon CloudFront (CDN) and Route 53 (DNS) close to users.
- **Local Zones, Wavelength Zones, AWS Outposts:** extend AWS closer to users, to 5G networks, or into your own data centre.

steps.title: Well-Architected Framework: six pillars
steps.body:
- **Operational excellence:** run and monitor systems, improve processes (automate, small frequent changes).
- **Security:** protect data and systems (least privilege, traceability, encryption).
- **Reliability:** recover from failure, scale to meet demand.
- **Performance efficiency:** use resources efficiently as demand and technology change.
- **Cost optimisation:** avoid unnecessary cost.
- **Sustainability:** minimise environmental impact of workloads.

steps.title: Benefits and migration strategies
steps.body:
Benefits often stated for cloud: trade fixed expense for variable expense; benefit from massive economies of scale; stop guessing capacity; increase speed and agility; stop spending money running data centres; go global in minutes.
Common migration strategies (the '7 Rs'): **retire**, **retain**, **rehost** (lift-and-shift), **relocate**, **repurchase** (move to SaaS), **replatform** (lift-tinker-shift, e.g. move a database to a managed service), **refactor/re-architect** (rebuild cloud-native).
The **AWS Cloud Adoption Framework** organises guidance into perspectives: business, people, governance, platform, security, operations.

steps.title: Worked example: applying the pillars
steps.body:
Aman and Sophia's app:
- Reliability: run web servers in at least two AZs behind a load balancer, with Auto Scaling.
- Performance: CloudFront caches video segments at edge locations.
- Cost: scale down at night; use Spot Instances for video transcoding jobs that can be interrupted.
- Security: MFA on the root user, least-privilege IAM roles, encryption at rest.
- Operational excellence: infrastructure as code and automated deployments.
- Sustainability: right-size instances; delete unused data.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick an app you use daily. Name one concrete improvement for each of the six Well-Architected pillars.

activity.prompt: Match each migration strategy to its example.
pairs: Move a VM as-is to Amazon EC2
Move a self-managed database to Amazon RDS with few code changes
Rebuild a monolith as serverless microservices
Replace an on-premises CRM with a SaaS product
Switch off an application nobody uses
Keep a system on-premises for now

quiz.q: For high availability within a Region, deploy across…
quiz.why: Availability Zones are isolated from each other's failures, so spreading across multiple AZs in a Region gives high availability. One large instance is a single point of failure.

quiz.q: Which pillar focuses on minimising environmental impact?
quiz.why: Sustainability is the sixth Well-Architected pillar. It focuses on minimising environmental impact.

quiz.q: Amazon CloudFront uses ___ to serve content close to users.
quiz.why: CloudFront is a CDN that serves content from edge locations, close to users. This reduces latency.

quiz.q: Moving a database to a managed service with minimal code change is…
quiz.why: Moving a database to a managed service with minimal code change is replatform ('lift, tinker and shift'). Rehost is a plain lift-and-shift.

quiz.q: A key factor when choosing a Region is…
options: Data residency, latency, services and price
quiz.why: Region choice depends on data residency and compliance, latency to users, available services and price. The number of edge locations is not the main factor.

lessons.title: Security, IAM and the shared responsibility model

story.title: The root password on a sticky note

scenes.text: At a small accounting firm in Surat, the AWS root user password was on a sticky note, and everyone used it.
One evening, unexpected EC2 instances appeared in several Regions — someone was mining cryptocurrency on the firm's bill.

Consultant Aditi locked it down: MFA on root, root used only for rare account tasks, individual identities through IAM Identity Center, least-privilege roles, CloudTrail logging everywhere and GuardDuty alerts.

steps.title: Shared responsibility
steps.body:
- **AWS: security OF the cloud** — hardware, global infrastructure, the software that runs managed services, physical security.
- **Customer: security IN the cloud** — data, identity and access management, OS patching on EC2, network and firewall configuration (security groups), encryption choices, application security.
The split shifts by service: for EC2 you patch the guest OS; for a managed service like Amazon RDS or AWS Lambda, AWS handles more of the underlying platform.

steps.title: IAM fundamentals
steps.body:
- **Root user:** created with the account; full access. Enable MFA, don't use it for everyday tasks, don't create access keys for it.
- **IAM users** (long-term credentials), **groups** (collections of users), **roles** (temporary credentials assumed by people, applications or AWS services — preferred for workloads, e.g. an EC2 instance role).
- **Policies** are JSON documents with Effect (Allow/Deny), Action, Resource and optional Condition. By default everything is **implicitly denied**; an **explicit deny always overrides** any allow.
- **IAM Identity Center** gives workforce users single sign-on across multiple accounts.
- Best practices: least privilege, MFA, roles instead of long-term keys, rotate credentials, review with IAM Access Analyzer.

steps.title: Worked example: reading a policy
steps.body:
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::invoices-2025/*
Effect: Deny, Action: s3:*, Resource: *, Condition: aws:SecureTransport = false
Meaning: the principal may read objects in the invoices-2025 bucket, but any S3 request not made over HTTPS is explicitly denied — even GetObject.

steps.title: Security and governance services
steps.body:
- **AWS Organizations:** manage multiple accounts; **service control policies (SCPs)** set the maximum permissions for accounts in an organisational unit.
- **AWS CloudTrail:** records API calls — who did what, when, from where.
- **AWS Config:** records resource configurations over time and checks compliance rules.
- **Amazon GuardDuty:** intelligent threat detection from logs.
- **Amazon Inspector:** automated vulnerability scanning of workloads.
- **Amazon Macie:** discovers sensitive data in S3.
- **AWS Shield:** DDoS protection (Standard is automatic; Advanced is a paid tier). **AWS WAF:** web application firewall rules.
- **AWS KMS:** manage encryption keys; **AWS Secrets Manager:** store and rotate secrets.
- **AWS Security Hub:** central view of security findings. **AWS Artifact:** download compliance reports and agreements.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Using the root user for daily work.
- Embedding access keys in code or public repositories — bots scan for them within minutes.
- Confusing CloudTrail (API activity) with CloudWatch (performance metrics/logs) and Config (configuration history).
- Thinking an SCP grants permissions — it only limits what IAM policies can allow.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For a new AWS account, list the first five security actions you would take, in order. (A good start: MFA on root; create an admin identity via Identity Center; enable CloudTrail in all Regions; set a billing alarm/budget; enable GuardDuty.)

activity.prompt: AWS or customer responsibility?

items.text: Patching the guest OS on an EC2 instance
Encrypting sensitive data stored in S3

quiz.q: Which statement about the root user is best practice?
options: Enable MFA and use it only for tasks that require it
quiz.why: Best practice is to enable MFA on the root user and use it only for the few tasks that need it. Do not share it or create access keys for it.

quiz.q: An IAM policy allows s3:* but another attached policy explicitly denies s3:DeleteObject. Can the user delete objects?
quiz.why: An explicit deny always overrides an allow in IAM. So the user cannot delete objects even though s3:* is allowed.

quiz.q: Which service shows who terminated an EC2 instance?
quiz.why: CloudTrail records API calls, including who terminated an EC2 instance. CloudWatch is for metrics and logs.

quiz.q: Limit the maximum permissions of all accounts in an organisational unit — use…
quiz.why: Service control policies (SCPs) in AWS Organizations set the maximum permissions for all accounts in an OU. They are guardrails and do not grant permissions themselves.

quiz.q: Where do you download AWS compliance reports such as ISO certifications?
quiz.why: AWS Artifact is the portal for downloading AWS compliance reports and agreements, such as ISO certifications.

lessons.title: Core services: compute, storage, databases and networking

scenes.text: A coaching institute in Kota hosted mock tests, videos and results on one old server. On result days, it collapsed.

Architect Nikhil rebuilt it on AWS: EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, videos in S3 delivered through CloudFront, student data in Amazon RDS, and a Lambda function generating score reports.
Databases lived in private subnets; only the load balancer was internet-facing.

steps.title: Compute
steps.body:
- **Amazon EC2:** virtual servers (instances); instance families for general purpose, compute, memory, storage, accelerated computing. Use **Auto Scaling** groups and **Elastic Load Balancing** (Application Load Balancer for HTTP/HTTPS layer 7; Network Load Balancer for TCP/UDP layer 4; Gateway Load Balancer for appliances).
- **AWS Lambda:** run code in response to events without managing servers; pay per request and duration.
- **Containers:** Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS (Kubernetes) orchestrate containers; **AWS Fargate** runs containers without managing servers; images in Amazon ECR.
- **AWS Elastic Beanstalk:** deploy web apps; AWS provisions the infrastructure.
- **Amazon Lightsail:** simple virtual servers with predictable pricing.

steps.title: Storage
steps.body:
- **Amazon S3:** object storage in buckets; designed for very high durability (eleven nines). Storage classes: S3 Standard, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 Standard-IA, S3 One Zone-IA, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, S3 Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest, retrieval in hours). Lifecycle rules move objects between classes. Versioning, replication, Block Public Access.
- **Amazon EBS:** block storage volumes for EC2 (in one AZ); snapshots stored durably.
- **EC2 instance store:** temporary block storage physically attached; data lost when the instance stops.
- **Amazon EFS:** shared, elastic NFS file system for Linux; **Amazon FSx** for Windows File Server, Lustre and others.
- **AWS Storage Gateway:** hybrid access to cloud storage; **AWS Snow Family** for offline data transfer; **AWS Backup** for centralised backups.

steps.title: Databases and analytics
steps.body:
- **Amazon RDS:** managed relational databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2); Multi-AZ deployments for high availability; read replicas for read scaling.
- **Amazon Aurora:** AWS's MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible high-performance relational database.
- **Amazon DynamoDB:** serverless key-value/document NoSQL with single-digit-millisecond performance at scale.
- **Amazon ElastiCache** (in-memory caching), **Amazon Redshift** (data warehouse), **Amazon Neptune** (graph), **Amazon DocumentDB** (MongoDB-compatible).
- **AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)** to migrate databases.
- Analytics: **Amazon Athena** (SQL queries on S3), **AWS Glue** (ETL and data catalogue), **Amazon Kinesis** (streaming), **Amazon QuickSight** (BI).

steps.title: Networking
steps.body:
- **Amazon VPC:** your isolated network; **public subnets** (route to an internet gateway) and **private subnets**; **NAT gateway** lets private instances reach the internet outbound only.
- **Security groups:** instance-level, **stateful**, allow rules only.
- **Network ACLs:** subnet-level, **stateless**, allow and deny rules, evaluated in number order.
- **AWS Site-to-Site VPN** (over the internet) and **AWS Direct Connect** (dedicated private connection).
- **Amazon Route 53:** DNS and domain registration with routing policies (simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation…).
- **Amazon CloudFront:** CDN. **AWS Global Accelerator:** improves global application availability and performance over the AWS network.

steps.title: Worked example: picking services
steps.body:
- Store 5 years of exam answer scripts, rarely accessed, retrieval within 12 hours OK → **S3 Glacier Deep Archive**.
- Session data needing microsecond reads → **ElastiCache**.
- Run a resize-image function every time a photo is uploaded → **Lambda** triggered by an S3 event.
- Relational database that must survive an AZ failure automatically → **RDS Multi-AZ**.
- Shared file system for 20 Linux web servers → **EFS**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Sketch the Kota portal: which parts sit in public subnets and which in private subnets? Where do security groups go? Label each service.

activity.prompt: Match the need to the AWS service.
pairs: Block storage volume for one EC2 instance
Dedicated private connection from office to AWS

quiz.q: Which firewall is stateful and works at the instance level?
quiz.why: A security group is a stateful firewall at the instance (network interface) level. Network ACLs are stateless and work at subnet level.

quiz.q: Cheapest S3 class for archives retrieved rarely with hours of delay acceptable?
quiz.why: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost storage class, meant for archives that are rarely retrieved, where hours of delay are fine.

quiz.q: Private instances need to download OS updates without being reachable from the internet. Use…
quiz.why: A NAT gateway lets private instances start outbound connections (e.g. updates) while staying unreachable from the internet. An internet gateway on their subnet would make them public.

quiz.q: A relational database must fail over automatically to another AZ. Choose…
quiz.why: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a standby in another AZ and fails over automatically. S3 versioning and EBS snapshots do not give automatic failover.

quiz.q: Run SQL queries directly on data in S3 without servers. Use…
quiz.why: Amazon Athena is a serverless service that runs SQL queries directly on data in S3, with no servers to manage.

story.title: Cutting the cloud bill by half

scenes.text: A food-delivery start-up in Lucknow saw its AWS bill grow faster than orders. Finance lead Kavita asked engineer Rahul to explain it.
Cost Explorer showed always-on EC2 instances, unattached EBS volumes and a test environment running 24×7.
They bought a Savings Plan for the steady baseline, moved batch jobs to Spot Instances, deleted waste and set AWS Budgets alerts. The bill dropped sharply within two months.

steps.title: EC2 pricing models
steps.body:
- **On-Demand:** pay by the second/hour, no commitment — for unpredictable or short workloads.
- **Savings Plans:** commit to a consistent amount of usage ($/hour) for 1 or 3 years in exchange for lower prices; Compute Savings Plans are flexible across instance families, Regions and also apply to Fargate and Lambda.
- **Reserved Instances:** 1- or 3-year commitment for specific instance attributes; discounts vs On-Demand.
- **Spot Instances:** spare capacity at steep discounts; AWS can reclaim them with a two-minute warning — for fault-tolerant, flexible jobs (batch, rendering, CI).
- **Dedicated Hosts / Dedicated Instances:** physical isolation, e.g. for licensing or compliance.
Also: data transfer *into* AWS is generally free; data transfer *out* to the internet is generally charged.

steps.title: Cost tools
steps.body:
- **AWS Pricing Calculator:** estimate costs before you build.
- **AWS Cost Explorer:** visualise and analyse historical spend and forecasts.
- **AWS Budgets:** set budgets and get alerts (cost, usage, reservation and Savings Plans coverage).
- **AWS Cost and Usage Report / data exports:** most detailed billing data.
- **Cost allocation tags:** attribute costs to teams or projects.
- **AWS Organizations consolidated billing:** one bill for many accounts; usage can be combined for volume pricing tiers.
- **AWS Free Tier:** limited free usage offers for new and existing customers (check current terms).
- **AWS Trusted Advisor:** checks for cost optimisation, security, fault tolerance, performance and service limits (the full set of checks comes with higher support plans).

steps.title: Support plans
steps.body:
- **Basic:** included for all accounts — documentation, forums, account and billing support, core Trusted Advisor checks, Personal Health Dashboard.
- **Developer:** business-hours technical support by email for experimentation.
- **Business:** 24×7 phone, email and chat support for production workloads; full Trusted Advisor checks.
- **Enterprise On-Ramp:** for business-critical workloads; access to a pool of Technical Account Managers.
- **Enterprise:** for mission-critical workloads; a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and the fastest response targets.
Other help: **AWS Marketplace** (third-party software), AWS Professional Services and Partner Network, AWS re:Post community, AWS Health Dashboard.

steps.title: Worked example: matching workloads to pricing
steps.body:
- Web servers running all year at a steady baseline of 10 instances → **Savings Plan** (or Reserved Instances) for the baseline + **On-Demand** for peaks.
- Nightly video transcoding that can restart if interrupted → **Spot**.
- A 3-week marketing microsite → **On-Demand**.
- Software licensed per physical server → **Dedicated Host**.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Confusing Cost Explorer (analyse past/forecast) with the Pricing Calculator (estimate new designs).
- Using Spot for a database that must never be interrupted.
- Forgetting unattached EBS volumes, idle load balancers and old snapshots — they still cost money.
- Assuming the Basic plan includes 24×7 technical phone support — it doesn't.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Create a zero-spend or small-amount budget alert in a practice account today. Then list three resources you would check monthly for waste.

a.text: You are Kavita. Rendering jobs run every night; they can be restarted if interrupted. Which pricing model saves most?

choices.label: Spot Instances
choices.feedback: Yes — interruptible, flexible work suits Spot.

choices.label: Dedicated Hosts
choices.feedback: Dedicated Hosts are for isolation/licensing, and are expensive.

b.text: The core order API runs 24×7 on a stable number of instances for the next 3 years. Best choice?

choices.label: Savings Plan or Reserved Instances for the steady baseline
choices.feedback: Commitment discounts fit steady, predictable usage.

choices.label: All On-Demand
choices.feedback: Works, but you pay the highest rate for a predictable load.

c.text: The bill goes up instead of down.

c2.text: Cost Explorer shows the API is your largest steady cost, and Savings Plans recommendations appear.

choices.label: Buy a Savings Plan for the baseline

d.text: Spot for batch, Savings Plan for the baseline, On-Demand for peaks, Budgets alerts and monthly waste reviews. A balanced cost strategy.

quiz.q: Which tool estimates the cost of a planned architecture?
quiz.why: The AWS Pricing Calculator estimates the cost of a planned architecture before you build it. Cost Explorer looks at costs you already incurred.

quiz.q: Spot Instances can be interrupted with how much warning?
quiz.why: Spot Instances can be interrupted by AWS with a two-minute warning. They are cheap but not for workloads that cannot stop.

quiz.q: Which support plan provides a designated Technical Account Manager?
quiz.why: The Enterprise support plan includes a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM). The lower plans do not.

quiz.q: Get alerts when monthly spend is forecast to exceed ₹50,000 — use…
quiz.why: AWS Budgets can alert you on actual or forecast spending crossing a threshold, such as ₹50,000 a month.

quiz.q: Consolidated billing is a feature of…
quiz.why: Consolidated billing, one bill for many accounts, is a feature of AWS Organizations. It can also combine usage for volume discounts.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of the cloud?
options: Trade fixed expense for variable expense
questions.why: A cloud benefit is trading fixed expense for variable expense: you pay for what you use instead of buying servers upfront.
Amazon S3 is the object storage service. EBS is block storage and RDS is a database service.

questions.q: Who patches the guest OS of an EC2 instance?
questions.why: Under the shared responsibility model, the customer secures what is 'in' the cloud, including patching the guest OS on EC2. AWS handles the underlying infrastructure.

questions.q: Which service records API calls for auditing?
questions.why: CloudTrail records API calls for auditing. AWS Config tracks resource configuration, and CloudFront is a CDN.

questions.q: A CDN service on AWS is…
questions.why: Amazon CloudFront is AWS's content delivery network (CDN). EFS is file storage and Direct Connect is a private network link.

questions.q: Which pricing option fits a steady workload over 3 years?
questions.why: For a steady workload over 3 years, commit with Savings Plans or Reserved Instances to get large discounts. On-Demand costs more and Spot can be interrupted.

questions.q: Which firewall is stateless and applies at the subnet level?
questions.why: A network ACL is stateless and applies at the subnet level. A security group is stateful and works at the instance level.

questions.q: A company wants automated threat detection from account and network logs. Use…
questions.why: Amazon GuardDuty detects threats automatically by analysing account activity and network logs.

questions.q: Discover personally identifiable information stored in S3 buckets — use…
questions.why: Amazon Macie uses machine learning to discover sensitive data, such as personally identifiable information, in S3 buckets.

questions.q: Applications on EC2 need to access S3 without stored access keys. Best practice?
options: Attach an IAM role to the instance
questions.why: Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance. It provides temporary credentials, so no keys are stored in code, and the bucket stays private.

questions.q: Which statement about SCPs is correct?
options: They set maximum available permissions for accounts
questions.why: SCPs set the maximum permissions available to accounts in an organisation. They do not grant permissions by themselves.

questions.q: Which Well-Architected pillar covers recovering from failures and meeting demand?
questions.why: The Reliability pillar covers recovering from failures and meeting demand. Sustainability is about environmental impact.

questions.q: Scenario: a shared file system for many Linux EC2 instances across AZs, growing automatically. Choose…
questions.why: Amazon EFS is a shared, elastic file system for Linux that many EC2 instances can use across AZs, and it grows automatically. EBS attaches to one instance in one AZ.

questions.q: Scenario: you must review whether a resource configuration complied with a rule last Tuesday. Use…
questions.why: AWS Config records configuration history and checks compliance with rules. So you can see whether a resource complied last Tuesday.

courses.title: Google Cloud Associate Cloud Engineer essentials
courses.summary: Set up projects and billing, manage IAM and service accounts, choose and deploy compute, storage, databases and networking, and operate with gcloud, logging and monitoring on Google Cloud. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can design the resource hierarchy and link billing, budgets and exports
Learners can grant IAM roles correctly and manage service accounts safely
Learners can choose between Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run, App Engine and Cloud Run functions
Learners can choose storage classes and databases, configure VPCs and firewall rules, and use gcloud, Logging and Monitoring

scenes.text: A media company in Noida had 20 Google Cloud projects created by different teams, all linked to one billing account, with everyone holding the Editor role.
Platform engineer Riya reorganised: an organisation node, folders for each business unit and environment, and projects beneath.
She replaced broad basic roles with predefined roles granted to Google Groups, set budgets with alerts per folder, and exported billing data to BigQuery for analysis.

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline. Google Cloud product names change (for example, Cloud Functions is now part of Cloud Run as Cloud Run functions) — verify in current documentation.

steps.title: The resource hierarchy
steps.body:
**Organization** (tied to a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain) → **Folders** (can nest; e.g. by department or environment) → **Projects** → **Resources**.
- A **project** is the base unit for enabling APIs, billing, and IAM; every resource belongs to one project.
- Each project has a **project name** (changeable), a **project ID** (globally unique, chosen at creation, cannot be changed) and a **project number** (assigned by Google).
- **Organization policies** (constraints) restrict configurations across the hierarchy, e.g. allowed resource locations, disabling service-account key creation.

steps.title: IAM: who can do what on which resource
steps.body:
- **Principals:** Google accounts, **Google Groups**, service accounts, Cloud Identity / Workspace domains.
- **Roles:**
  - **Basic:** Owner, Editor, Viewer — very broad; avoid in production.
  - **Predefined:** fine-grained, service-specific (e.g. roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1, roles/storage.objectViewer).
  - **Custom:** your own permission sets.
- An **allow policy** binds principals to roles on a resource; policies are **inherited** down the hierarchy, and the effective policy is the union of the resource's policy and its ancestors'.
- Grant roles to **groups**, not individuals; apply least privilege.

steps.title: Service accounts
steps.body:
- A **service account** is an identity for workloads (a VM, a Cloud Run service, a pipeline).
- Attach a service account to the resource so code gets credentials automatically; avoid downloading **service account keys** — they are long-lived secrets. For external workloads (other clouds, CI systems), prefer **Workload Identity Federation**.
- A service account is both an identity (it can be granted roles) and a resource (you can control who can use or impersonate it, e.g. roles/iam.serviceAccountUser).

steps.title: Billing
steps.body:
- A **Cloud Billing account** pays for one or more projects; linking a project to a billing account requires appropriate billing permissions (e.g. Billing Account User on the billing account plus permission on the project).
- **Budgets and alerts** notify at thresholds (they do not cap spending by themselves; you can automate responses via Pub/Sub notifications).
- **Billing export to BigQuery** for detailed analysis; labels on resources help attribute cost.

steps.title: Worked example: gcloud basics
steps.body:
gcloud auth login
gcloud config set project media-prod-123
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding media-prod-123 --member='group:video-ops@example.com' --role='roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1'
gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com

Cloud Shell in the console has gcloud preinstalled — ideal for practice.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Design a hierarchy for a company with Retail and Logistics units, each with dev and prod. Where would you set an organization policy restricting resource locations to Indian regions?

statements.s: A project ID can be changed after the project is created.
statements.why: Project IDs are permanent; the display name can change.

statements.s: IAM policies set on a folder are inherited by projects inside it.
Basic roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) are recommended for production least privilege.
Downloading service account keys is the preferred way for VMs to authenticate.
statements.why: Attach the service account to the VM instead.

statements.s: A budget alert automatically stops all resources.

quiz.q: The base unit for enabling APIs and billing in Google Cloud is…
quiz.why: A project is the base unit in Google Cloud for enabling APIs, billing and resources. Folders and the organisation sit above it.

quiz.q: Best way to give 15 operators the same access?
options: Grant the role to a Google Group
quiz.why: Grant the role to a Google Group and add the 15 operators to it. This is simpler to manage than granting each one individually.

quiz.q: Which role type is most fine-grained among Google-managed roles?
quiz.why: Predefined roles are service-specific and fine-grained, managed by Google. Basic roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) are very broad.

quiz.q: A CI system in another cloud must deploy to Google Cloud without stored keys. Use…
options: Service account key in the CI
quiz.why: Workload Identity Federation lets an external system exchange its own token for short-lived Google credentials. This avoids storing service account keys.

quiz.q: Analyse detailed billing data with SQL — enable…
quiz.why: Export billing data to BigQuery to analyse detailed costs with SQL.

lessons.title: Compute options: Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run and App Engine

scenes.text: A retail chain in Chennai had a legacy inventory app, a set of containerised microservices, and a small webhook that processed payment notifications.
Cloud engineer Karthik put the legacy app on Compute Engine managed instance groups, the microservices on GKE Autopilot, and the webhook on Cloud Run, which scales to zero when idle.
The webhook cost almost nothing on quiet days, and the inventory app healed itself when a VM failed.

steps.title: Compute Engine
steps.body:
- VMs with predefined or custom **machine types** (e.g. E2, N2, C-series, memory-optimised).
- **Spot VMs** (and the older preemptible VMs): much cheaper, can be stopped by Google at any time — for fault-tolerant batch jobs.
- **Instance templates** + **managed instance groups (MIGs):** identical VMs with **autoscaling**, **autohealing** (health checks recreate failed VMs) and rolling updates; regional MIGs spread across zones.
- Disks: Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk options; snapshots and images. **Sole-tenant nodes** for dedicated hardware.
- Example: gcloud compute instances create web-1 --zone=asia-south1-a --machine-type=e2-medium

steps.title: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
steps.body:
- Managed Kubernetes. **Autopilot** mode: Google manages nodes; you pay for pod resources. **Standard** mode: you manage node pools for more control.
- Regional clusters replicate the control plane and nodes across zones.
- Typical commands: gcloud container clusters create-auto shop --region=asia-south1, then kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml.
- Images usually come from **Artifact Registry**.

steps.title: Serverless: Cloud Run and App Engine
steps.body:
- **Cloud Run:** run stateless containers that scale automatically (including to zero), billed by usage; services for HTTP and jobs for run-to-completion tasks. Revisions and traffic splitting enable gradual rollouts.
- **Cloud Run functions** (formerly Cloud Functions): deploy single-purpose functions triggered by HTTP or events (Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, Eventarc).
- **App Engine:** platform for web apps — **standard** environment (sandboxed runtimes, fast scaling, scale to zero) and **flexible** environment (runs in containers on VMs). An App Engine application's region cannot be changed after creation.

steps.title: Worked example: choosing compute
steps.body:
- Lift-and-shift Windows app with custom drivers → **Compute Engine**.
- 30 microservices, need Kubernetes APIs → **GKE** (Autopilot to reduce ops).
- Containerised API with spiky traffic, minimal ops → **Cloud Run**.
- Resize an image when a file lands in a bucket → **Cloud Run functions** with a Cloud Storage trigger.
- Overnight rendering, interruptions acceptable → **Spot VMs** in a MIG.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Running a stateful database on Spot VMs.
- Forgetting health checks on MIGs (no autohealing).
- Choosing GKE Standard when the team has no Kubernetes operations experience — Autopilot or Cloud Run may fit better.
- Expecting Cloud Run to keep in-memory state between requests — design stateless services.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In Cloud Shell: deploy a sample container to Cloud Run with gcloud run deploy, open the URL, then deploy a second revision and split traffic 90/10.

activity.prompt: Match the workload to the compute option.
pairs: Legacy app needing full OS control
Stateless container API that scales to zero
Function triggered by a file upload

quiz.q: Which feature recreates failed VMs automatically?
options: Autohealing in a managed instance group
quiz.why: Autohealing in a managed instance group uses health checks to recreate VMs that fail.

quiz.q: In GKE Autopilot, who manages the nodes?
quiz.why: In GKE Autopilot, Google manages the nodes and the underlying infrastructure. You only manage workloads.

quiz.q: A containerised API has unpredictable spikes and must cost little when idle. Choose…
quiz.why: Cloud Run runs containers serverlessly. It scales with traffic, even down to zero, so cost is little when idle.

quiz.q: Can an App Engine application's region be changed after creation?
quiz.why: The region of an App Engine application is chosen at creation and cannot be changed afterwards.
Spot VMs are cheap but can be reclaimed at any time. They suit fault-tolerant batch jobs, not services that need guaranteed uptime.

scenes.text: A ride-hailing start-up in Pune stored trip receipts, driver documents, live locations and analytics — all in one MySQL database. It was slow and expensive.
Data engineer Neha split it: documents in Cloud Storage with lifecycle rules, live locations in Bigtable, the transactional core in Cloud SQL, and analytics in BigQuery.
When they expanded to other countries needing globally consistent bookings, they evaluated Spanner.

steps.title: Cloud Storage
steps.body:
- Object storage in **buckets** (bucket names are globally unique). Location types: **region**, **dual-region**, **multi-region**.
- **Storage classes:** Standard (hot data), **Nearline** (minimum 30 days; about once a month), **Coldline** (minimum 90 days; about once a quarter), **Archive** (minimum 365 days; less than once a year). Unlike some archive services elsewhere, data in all classes is available with low latency — colder classes have higher retrieval costs and minimum durations.
- **Object Lifecycle Management** changes class or deletes objects by age and conditions; **Autoclass** can manage classes automatically.
- Access: IAM (prefer **uniform bucket-level access**), **signed URLs** for time-limited access; object versioning; retention policies and bucket lock for compliance.
- CLI: gcloud storage cp file.pdf gs://bucket-name/ (older tool: gsutil).

steps.title: Block and file storage
steps.body:
- **Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk:** durable block storage for VMs (zonal or regional replication options); snapshots.
- **Local SSD:** very fast, temporary, physically attached — data is lost when the VM stops.
- **Filestore:** managed NFS file shares.

steps.title: Databases — choose by data shape
steps.body:
- **Cloud SQL:** managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server — regional relational workloads; high availability configuration and read replicas.
- **AlloyDB for PostgreSQL:** high-performance PostgreSQL-compatible database.
- **Spanner:** relational, horizontally scalable, strongly consistent, can be multi-regional — global transactional systems.
- **Bigtable:** wide-column NoSQL for very high throughput and low latency (time-series, IoT, ad-tech); HBase-compatible API.
- **Firestore:** serverless document database for web/mobile apps with real-time sync.
- **Memorystore:** managed Redis/Memcached-compatible caching.
- **BigQuery:** serverless data warehouse for SQL analytics at large scale; you pay for storage and queries (on-demand by bytes processed, or capacity pricing).

steps.title: Worked example: decision flow
steps.body:
- Need SQL joins and transactions?
  - Single region, standard engines → **Cloud SQL**.
  - Global scale, strong consistency → **Spanner**.
- No relational needs?
  - Massive time-series writes with key lookups → **Bigtable**.
  - App documents with offline/mobile sync → **Firestore**.
- Analytics over terabytes with SQL → **BigQuery**.
- Files/objects (images, PDFs, backups) → **Cloud Storage**.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Using Bigtable for small datasets or for complex relational queries.
- Running SELECT * on huge BigQuery tables — you pay for bytes scanned; select only needed columns and use partitioned/clustered tables.
- Putting data accessed daily into Archive class — retrieval fees and the 365-day minimum add up.
- Forgetting that Local SSD data does not survive VM stops.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Create a bucket, upload a file, add a lifecycle rule (to Nearline after 30 days, delete after 400 days), and generate a signed URL valid for 10 minutes.

activity.prompt: Pick the best Google Cloud data service.

items.text: Billions of GPS pings per day keyed by vehicle and time
SQL analytics on two years of trip data
Backups kept for 7 years, rarely read

quiz.why: Minimum storage durations: Nearline 30 days, Coldline 90 days, Archive 365 days. Early deletion is charged for the remaining time.

quiz.q: Which database is globally distributed, relational and strongly consistent?
quiz.why: Spanner is Google's globally distributed relational database with strong consistency. Cloud SQL is regional, and Firestore is a NoSQL document database.

quiz.q: Give a partner 15-minute access to one object without a Google account. Use…
quiz.why: A signed URL gives time-limited access to an object without needing a Google account. A public bucket would expose everything.

quiz.q: How to reduce BigQuery on-demand query cost?
options: Query only needed columns and use partitioned tables
quiz.why: BigQuery on-demand pricing is by bytes scanned. Select only the columns you need and use partitioned tables to scan less. SELECT * scans every column.

quiz.q: High-throughput time-series writes with key lookups fit…
quiz.why: Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL database built for high-throughput writes and key lookups, such as time-series data.

story.title: The VM nobody could SSH into

scenes.text: Engineer Ishaan in Hyderabad created a VM in a new custom VPC and couldn't SSH into it. The default network he had used before had worked fine.

His senior, Maria, explained: custom VPCs have only the implied rules — allow all egress, deny all ingress. He needed a firewall rule allowing SSH, ideally only from Identity-Aware Proxy's address range.
Then they set up Cloud Monitoring alerts and log-based metrics so they'd know about problems before users did.

steps.title: VPC networks
steps.body:
- A Google Cloud **VPC network is global**; **subnets are regional**. One VPC can have subnets in Mumbai, Delhi and Singapore.
- **Auto mode** creates a subnet in every region automatically; **custom mode** lets you choose ranges (recommended for production).
- **Firewall rules** apply to the whole VPC and target instances by network tags or service accounts; priority 0–65535 (lower = higher priority). **Implied rules:** allow all egress, deny all ingress. (The 'default' network also comes with some pre-populated allow rules.)
- **Cloud NAT** gives private VMs outbound internet access; **Private Google Access** lets VMs without external IPs reach Google APIs.
- **Shared VPC:** a host project shares its VPC with service projects (central network control). **VPC Network Peering** connects VPCs privately (not transitive).
- Hybrid: **Cloud VPN** (IPsec) and **Cloud Interconnect** (dedicated or partner). **Cloud DNS** for public and private zones.
- **Cloud Load Balancing:** global and regional, external and internal options (HTTP(S), TCP/UDP).

steps.title: Operating with tools
steps.body:
- **Cloud Shell** and **gcloud** for automation; **Infrastructure as code** with Terraform (also via Google Cloud's Infrastructure Manager).
- **Cloud Logging:** collect, search and route logs (log sinks to BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub); **log-based metrics**.
- **Cloud Monitoring:** metrics, dashboards, uptime checks, **alerting policies** with notification channels.
- Audit logs: **Admin Activity** (always on), **Data Access** (often needs enabling), System Event, Policy Denied.
- **Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)** TCP forwarding enables SSH/RDP to VMs without external IPs.

steps.title: Worked example: a firewall rule for IAP SSH
steps.body:
gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-ssh-iap \
  --network=shop-vpc --direction=INGRESS --action=allow \
  --rules=tcp:22 --source-ranges=35.235.240.0/20 \
  --target-tags=ssh-allowed

Then add the network tag 'ssh-allowed' to the VM and connect with gcloud compute ssh web-1 --tunnel-through-iap. (35.235.240.0/20 is the range IAP uses for TCP forwarding; confirm in current docs.)

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Assuming subnets are global (they're regional) or VPCs are regional (they're global).
- Opening SSH (tcp:22) to 0.0.0.0/0 — prefer IAP or a bastion.
- Overlapping ranges when peering VPCs or connecting VPNs.
- Expecting Data Access audit logs to be on for every service by default.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Create a custom-mode VPC with one subnet in asia-south1, a VM without an external IP, the IAP firewall rule above, and connect via IAP. Then create an uptime check and an alerting policy.

a.text: You are Ishaan. A new VM in a custom VPC has no external IP. You need SSH access securely. What first?

choices.label: Firewall rule allowing tcp:22 from the IAP range, targeted by network tag
choices.feedback: Correct — then use IAP TCP forwarding.

choices.label: Allow tcp:22 from 0.0.0.0/0
choices.feedback: Opens SSH to the whole internet — and the VM has no external IP anyway.

b.text: The VM must download packages from the internet but stay without an external IP. Configure…

choices.label: Cloud NAT on the subnet's region
Give it an external IP
choices.feedback: Works but increases exposure; not required.

c.text: The security scanner flags an internet-wide SSH rule.

c2.text: The review asks why a private app server has a public IP.

choices.label: Remove it and use Cloud NAT

d.text: Private VM, IAP for admin access, Cloud NAT for outbound updates, monitoring alerts for health. Secure by default.

quiz.q: In Google Cloud, a VPC network is ___ and subnets are ___.
quiz.why: In Google Cloud a VPC network is global and its subnets are regional. This differs from AWS, where a VPC is regional.

quiz.q: Implied firewall rules in a VPC are…
options: Allow all egress, deny all ingress
quiz.why: The implied VPC firewall rules allow all egress and deny all ingress. You add allow rules to let traffic in.

quiz.q: Centralise network administration while letting teams use their own projects — use…
quiz.why: Shared VPC lets a host project provide the network, so network administration is central, while teams use their own service projects.

quiz.q: Route certain logs to BigQuery for analysis — create a…
quiz.why: A log sink routes selected logs to a destination such as BigQuery, Cloud Storage or Pub/Sub.

quiz.q: Private VMs need Google APIs (e.g. Cloud Storage) without external IPs. Enable…
quiz.why: Private Google Access lets VMs with only internal IPs reach Google APIs and services such as Cloud Storage. Public IPs are not needed.

questions.q: The top node of the Google Cloud resource hierarchy is…
questions.why: The organization is the top node of the Google Cloud resource hierarchy. Folders and projects are beneath it.

questions.q: Which service runs stateless containers serverlessly?
questions.why: Cloud Run runs stateless containers serverlessly. Spanner is a database and Filestore is file storage.

questions.q: Which CLI is the main command-line tool for Google Cloud?
questions.why: gcloud is the main command-line tool for Google Cloud. aws is for AWS and az for Azure.

questions.q: Which storage class has a 365-day minimum storage duration?
questions.why: Archive class has a 365-day minimum storage duration. Nearline is 30 days and Coldline is 90.

questions.q: Which identity should a VM's application use to call Google APIs?
options: A shared key file emailed around
questions.why: A VM's application should use an attached service account. This avoids passwords or key files that can leak.

questions.q: A team needs identical web VMs that scale with CPU and heal automatically. Use…
options: Managed instance group with autoscaling and health checks
questions.why: A managed instance group creates identical VMs from a template, with autoscaling on CPU and health checks for autohealing. An unmanaged group offers neither.

questions.q: Which database suits global, strongly consistent transactions?
questions.why: Spanner gives globally distributed, strongly consistent transactions. Bigtable is not relational and does not offer the same transactions.

questions.q: Restrict all projects to Indian regions. Use…
options: Organization policy constraint on resource locations
questions.why: An organization policy constraint on resource locations restricts where resources can be created, such as only Indian regions. IAM roles and firewall rules do not do this.

questions.q: VPC A peers with B, B peers with C. Can A reach C through B?
questions.why: VPC peering is not transitive. If A peers with B and B with C, A cannot reach C through B unless A and C are also peered.

questions.q: Which audit log type is always enabled and records configuration changes?
questions.why: Admin Activity audit logs are always on and record changes to configuration or metadata. Data Access logs must be enabled and can be large.

questions.q: Linking a project to a billing account requires…
options: Appropriate permissions on both the billing account (e.g. Billing Account User) and the project
questions.why: Linking a project to a billing account needs permission on both sides: for example Billing Account User on the billing account and permission to change billing on the project.

questions.q: Scenario: external CI must deploy without long-lived keys. Best option?
options: Owner role for the CI user
Service account key stored in CI secrets
questions.why: Workload Identity Federation gives the external CI short-lived credentials without a stored key. A stored service account key is long-lived and can leak.

questions.q: Scenario: BigQuery costs spike from analysts running SELECT * on a 10 TB table. Best first fix?
options: Partition/cluster the table and teach selecting needed columns; set custom quotas
questions.why: BigQuery bills by bytes scanned. Partition and cluster the table, teach analysts to select only needed columns, and set custom quotas to cap usage. Disabling BigQuery or moving to Cloud SQL does not solve it.

lessons.title: Service mapping: same ideas, different names

scenes.text: Pallavi had five years of Azure experience in Bengaluru. Her new employer ran mostly on AWS, with analytics on Google Cloud.
Instead of starting from zero, she built a mapping sheet: 'VM → EC2 → Compute Engine; Blob → S3 → Cloud Storage…'
Within two weeks she was reviewing designs. 'The ideas are the same,' she said. 'The names and a few important details differ.'

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline. Mappings are approximate — equivalent services differ in features, limits and pricing.

steps.title: Compute and containers
steps.body:
- Virtual machines: **Azure Virtual Machines** ↔ **Amazon EC2** ↔ **Compute Engine**.
- Auto-scaling groups: **VM Scale Sets** ↔ **EC2 Auto Scaling groups** ↔ **managed instance groups**.
- Web app platform: **App Service** ↔ **Elastic Beanstalk** ↔ **App Engine**.
- Functions: **Azure Functions** ↔ **AWS Lambda** ↔ **Cloud Run functions**.
- Serverless containers: **Azure Container Apps** ↔ **AWS Fargate / App Runner** ↔ **Cloud Run**.
- Kubernetes: **AKS** ↔ **Amazon EKS** ↔ **GKE**.
- Container registry: **Azure Container Registry** ↔ **Amazon ECR** ↔ **Artifact Registry**.

steps.title: Storage and databases
steps.body:
- Object storage: **Blob Storage** ↔ **Amazon S3** ↔ **Cloud Storage**.
- Block disks: **Managed Disks** ↔ **Amazon EBS** ↔ **Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk**.
- File shares: **Azure Files** ↔ **Amazon EFS / FSx** ↔ **Filestore**.
- Managed relational: **Azure SQL Database / Azure Database for PostgreSQL & MySQL** ↔ **Amazon RDS / Aurora** ↔ **Cloud SQL / AlloyDB**.
- Global relational: (Azure options include Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL and Azure SQL Hyperscale) ↔ (Aurora global database) ↔ **Spanner** — these differ significantly; compare carefully.
- NoSQL: **Cosmos DB** ↔ **DynamoDB** ↔ **Firestore / Bigtable**.
- Data warehouse: **Microsoft Fabric / Synapse** ↔ **Amazon Redshift** ↔ **BigQuery**.

steps.title: Networking, identity and management
steps.body:
- Private network: **VNet** ↔ **VPC** ↔ **VPC** (Google's is global; Azure VNets and AWS VPCs are regional).
- Dedicated link: **ExpressRoute** ↔ **Direct Connect** ↔ **Cloud Interconnect**.
- DNS: **Azure DNS** ↔ **Route 53** ↔ **Cloud DNS**. CDN: **Azure Front Door / CDN** ↔ **CloudFront** ↔ **Cloud CDN**.
- Identity: **Microsoft Entra ID** ↔ **IAM / IAM Identity Center** ↔ **Cloud Identity + IAM**.
- Secrets/keys: **Key Vault** ↔ **Secrets Manager / KMS** ↔ **Secret Manager / Cloud KMS**.
- Monitoring: **Azure Monitor** ↔ **CloudWatch** ↔ **Cloud Monitoring / Logging**. Audit: **Activity log** ↔ **CloudTrail** ↔ **Cloud Audit Logs**.
- Infrastructure as code: **ARM / Bicep** ↔ **CloudFormation** ↔ **Infrastructure Manager (Terraform)**; Terraform works on all three.
- Guardrails: **Azure Policy** ↔ **SCPs + AWS Config rules** ↔ **Organization Policy**.

steps.title: How to learn a second cloud quickly
steps.body:
- Map concepts first, then learn the **differences that bite**: account hierarchy, identity model, network scope, default security posture, pricing units.
- Rebuild one small project you know well (a three-tier app) on the new cloud.
- Read each provider's well-architected guidance; they share many principles.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Make your own three-column mapping sheet for 15 services you use at work or in study, and add one 'gotcha' difference for each.

cards.front: Azure Blob Storage = AWS ? = Google Cloud ?

cards.back: DynamoDB (closest) = Firestore / Bigtable depending on use
Secrets Manager / KMS = Secret Manager / Cloud KMS

quiz.q: Amazon EC2's Google Cloud equivalent is…
quiz.why: Amazon EC2 and Google Compute Engine are both virtual machine services.

quiz.q: Which provider's VPC network is global by default?
quiz.why: A Google Cloud VPC network is global by default, with regional subnets. AWS VPCs and Azure VNets are regional.
BigQuery is a serverless data warehouse, and the closest AWS service is Amazon Redshift.

quiz.q: Azure's audit of control-plane operations is the Activity log. AWS's equivalent is…
quiz.why: AWS CloudTrail records API activity, like the Azure Activity log does for control-plane operations.

quiz.q: Which IaC tool works across all three clouds?
quiz.why: Terraform has providers for AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. CloudFormation is AWS-only, while ARM and Bicep are Azure-only.

lessons.title: Accounts, identity and networks: the differences that bite

scenes.text: Pallavi assumed AWS security groups worked like Azure NSGs with deny rules. She tried to add a 'deny' rule to a security group — there was no such option.
Her colleague Marco explained: security groups are allow-only and stateful; for explicit denies at subnet level, AWS uses network ACLs.
She added it to her 'gotchas' sheet — the list that made her the team's go-to multi-cloud reviewer.

steps.title: Hierarchy and billing
steps.body:
- **Azure:** tenant (Entra ID) → management groups → subscriptions → resource groups → resources. Subscriptions are the billing/access boundary.
- **AWS:** AWS Organizations → organisational units (OUs) → **accounts** → resources. The account is the main isolation and billing unit; tags group resources.
- **Google Cloud:** organization → folders → **projects** → resources. Projects link to billing accounts.
Rough equivalents: subscription ≈ AWS account ≈ project; management group ≈ OU ≈ folder; resource group has no exact twin (AWS Resource Groups/tags, Google labels).

steps.title: Identity models
steps.body:
- **Azure:** Microsoft Entra ID for identities; Azure RBAC role assignments at scopes; managed identities for workloads.
- **AWS:** IAM users/groups/roles with JSON policies; explicit deny overrides; roles for workloads; IAM Identity Center for workforce SSO; SCPs as guardrails.
- **Google Cloud:** Google accounts/groups via Cloud Identity or Workspace; IAM allow policies bind roles at hierarchy levels; service accounts for workloads; Workload Identity Federation for external workloads.
Common principle everywhere: least privilege, groups over individuals, no long-lived keys in code.

steps.title: Network security differences
steps.body:
- **Azure NSG:** allow and deny rules with priorities; attach to subnet and/or NIC; stateful.
- **AWS security group:** allow-only, stateful, attached to instances/ENIs. **Network ACL:** allow and deny, stateless, subnet-level, numbered rules.
- **Google Cloud firewall rules:** VPC-wide, allow and deny, priorities, targeted by network tags or service accounts; stateful; implied deny ingress/allow egress; hierarchical firewall policies at org/folder level.
- Scope: Azure VNet and AWS VPC are regional; Google VPC is global with regional subnets.

steps.title: Worked example: 'block one bad IP'
steps.body:
- Azure: add an NSG rule 'Deny from 203.0.113.7' with a lower priority number than the allow rule.
- AWS: security groups can't deny; add a **network ACL** deny rule with a lower rule number on the subnet (or use AWS WAF for web traffic).
- Google Cloud: create a firewall rule action=deny from 203.0.113.7 with a higher priority (lower number) than the allow rule.
(203.0.113.0/24 is a documentation range used in examples.)

steps.title: Gotchas to remember
steps.body:
- Storage archive tiers behave differently: Azure Archive and S3 Glacier Flexible/Deep Archive need restore/rehydration time; Google Cloud Storage Archive is readable immediately but expensive to retrieve.
- Default networks differ: Google projects may come with a 'default' VPC with some open rules; review and often delete it.
- Free tiers, support plans and SLA calculations differ — never assume one provider's terms apply to another.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write how you'd grant a VM read access to object storage on each cloud without keys. (Azure: managed identity + Storage Blob Data Reader; AWS: instance role with s3:GetObject; Google: attached service account with roles/storage.objectViewer.)

statements.s: AWS security groups support explicit deny rules.
statements.why: They are allow-only; use network ACLs or WAF to deny.

statements.s: Google Cloud firewall rules can target instances by network tags.
An Azure subscription is roughly comparable to an AWS account or a Google Cloud project.
Google Cloud Storage Archive class requires hours of rehydration before reading.
statements.why: It's online; costs and minimum durations differ instead.
Return traffic must be allowed explicitly.

quiz.why: A Google folder is similar to an AWS organisational unit (OU) and an Azure management group. All are layers that group accounts, projects or subscriptions.

quiz.q: Workload identity without keys on AWS is done with…
quiz.why: On AWS, workloads use IAM roles to get temporary credentials without keys. Root keys should be avoided.
AWS network ACLs are stateless, so you must allow return traffic explicitly. Security groups, Azure NSGs and Google firewall rules are stateful.

quiz.q: Which cloud's VPC spans regions as one network?
quiz.why: Google Cloud's VPC is global, so it spans regions as one network. AWS VPCs and Azure VNets are regional.

quiz.q: Common identity principle across all three clouds?
options: Least privilege with groups and no long-lived keys in code
quiz.why: All three clouds share the principle of least privilege, using groups and avoiding long-lived keys in code.

lessons.title: Designing a three-tier app on any cloud, and when multi-cloud makes sense

scenes.text: The board of an insurance company in Mumbai heard 'multi-cloud' at a conference and asked CTO Deepa to run everything on three clouds.
Deepa's team compared costs, skills and risk. Running every app everywhere would triple operations work and complexity.

They chose a primary cloud for most workloads, a second cloud for analytics where it was strongest, and portable tooling (containers, Terraform, open standards) with a tested exit plan. The board agreed.

steps.title: The pattern
steps.body:
A classic three-tier web app:
- **Presentation:** CDN + global/regional HTTP load balancer with WAF.
- **Application:** auto-scaled compute (VM groups, containers or serverless) in private subnets across zones.
- **Data:** managed relational database with high availability + object storage + cache.
- **Cross-cutting:** identity for workloads, secrets store, logging/monitoring, backups, IaC and CI/CD.

steps.title: Worked example: one design, three clouds
steps.body:
- **Azure:** Front Door (WAF) → App Service or AKS in a VNet (zone-redundant) → Azure SQL (zone-redundant) + Blob Storage + Azure Cache for Redis; managed identities, Key Vault, Azure Monitor; Bicep + pipelines.
- **AWS:** CloudFront + ALB (WAF) → ECS on Fargate or EC2 Auto Scaling in private subnets across AZs → RDS Multi-AZ + S3 + ElastiCache; IAM roles, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch; CloudFormation/Terraform.
- **Google Cloud:** Cloud CDN + external HTTP(S) load balancer with Cloud Armor → Cloud Run or GKE (regional) → Cloud SQL (HA) + Cloud Storage + Memorystore; service accounts, Secret Manager, Cloud Monitoring; Terraform.

steps.title: Multi-cloud: reasons and costs
steps.body:
Good reasons: a specific service is much better on one cloud; regulatory or customer requirements; acquisitions; negotiating leverage; resilience for a few critical systems.
Costs: more skills to maintain, duplicated tooling, harder networking and identity, data-egress charges between clouds, inconsistent security controls.
Practical approach: **primary cloud + targeted use of others**, common tooling (Terraform, Kubernetes, OpenTelemetry), central identity and policy, and documented exit/portability plans.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Spreading one latency-sensitive app across clouds — cross-cloud traffic is slower and costs egress.
- Using only the lowest common denominator, losing each cloud's strengths.
- Inconsistent identity: separate admin accounts everywhere without SSO and MFA.
- No owner for cloud costs across providers.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Redraw the three-tier design for your favourite cloud with exact service names. Then list three things you'd need to change to move it to another cloud.

a.text: You are Deepa. The board wants 'everything on three clouds'. What do you propose?

choices.label: Primary cloud plus targeted use of others, with portable tooling and an exit plan
Run every app actively on all three clouds
choices.feedback: Triples operations work and egress costs for most apps.

b.text: Analytics would benefit from another cloud's data warehouse. Your main concern?

choices.label: Data egress cost and governance of data moving between clouds
choices.feedback: Exactly — plan data movement, security and cost.

c.text: Six months in: three on-call rotations, inconsistent security, ballooning bills.

choices.label: Consolidate to a primary cloud with targeted exceptions

c2.text: The first month's inter-cloud data transfer bill surprises finance.

choices.label: Redesign data flows and estimate egress upfront

d.text: A clear multi-cloud strategy: one primary platform, analytics where it is strongest, central identity and policy, Terraform everywhere, and costs owned and tracked.

quiz.q: Which is generally a valid reason for multi-cloud?
options: A specific service is clearly better on another cloud
quiz.why: Multi-cloud is a valid choice when a specific service is clearly better on another cloud. Doing it only because it is trendy adds complexity.

quiz.q: A hidden cost of splitting one app across clouds is…
quiz.why: Splitting an app across clouds creates data egress charges and extra latency, because cross-cloud traffic costs money and time.

quiz.q: Which tool helps keep observability consistent across clouds?
quiz.why: OpenTelemetry is an open standard for traces, metrics and logs, so observability can be consistent across clouds.

quiz.q: In the AWS version of the three-tier design, the managed HA relational database is…
quiz.why: In the AWS three-tier design, the managed highly available relational database is Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ.

quiz.q: Google Cloud's WAF/DDoS protection service for load balancers is…
quiz.why: Cloud Armor is Google Cloud's WAF and DDoS protection for load balancers. Cloud NAT is for outbound access.

questions.why: Amazon S3's Azure equivalent is Blob Storage. Both are object storage.
GKE is Google's managed Kubernetes. The AWS equivalent is Amazon EKS.

questions.q: Which is Google Cloud's dedicated private connection service?
questions.why: Cloud Interconnect is Google Cloud's dedicated private connection to on-premises networks. Cloud CDN is for content delivery.

questions.q: The AWS unit roughly equivalent to an Azure subscription is…
questions.why: An AWS account is roughly the same as an Azure subscription, as the basic billing and isolation unit.

questions.q: Azure Policy's closest Google Cloud counterpart is…
questions.why: Azure Policy sets rules and constraints on resource configuration. Google's closest counterpart is Organization Policy.

questions.q: To block a single IP in AWS at subnet level you use…
questions.why: AWS security groups only have allow rules, so to block a single IP at subnet level you use a network ACL deny rule.

options: Google VPCs are global; Azure VNets and AWS VPCs are regional
All three clouds' VPCs are global
questions.why: Google VPCs are global, while Azure VNets and AWS VPCs are regional. This is an important design difference.

questions.q: Grant a Google Cloud VM read access to buckets without keys — use…
options: An attached service account with a storage viewer role
A signed URL for every object forever
questions.why: Attach a service account with a storage viewer role to the VM. It provides credentials without keys or passwords.

questions.q: Which archive storage behaves differently by being immediately readable (with high retrieval cost)?
questions.why: Google's Cloud Storage Archive class is online: data is readable immediately, although retrieval costs more. Azure Archive and S3 Glacier Deep Archive need restoring first.

questions.q: Scenario: a latency-sensitive API in AWS calls a database in Google Cloud for every request. Main risks?
options: Added latency, egress charges and more complex security
questions.why: Calling a database in another cloud for every request adds latency and egress charges, and it makes security more complex.

questions.q: Scenario: a company wants portability between clouds for its app tier. A practical choice?
options: Containers + Kubernetes/Cloud Run-style platforms and Terraform for infrastructure
Write everything in provider-specific templates only
Use only VMs with manual setup
questions.why: Containers on Kubernetes or Cloud Run-style platforms with Terraform improve portability, because they use common abstractions. Provider-specific templates tie you to one cloud.

lessons.title: Cloud concepts: why the cloud, and who is responsible for what

scenes.text: Rekha runs an online sweets shop in Kolkata. Every Diwali her single office server crashed under the traffic, and the rest of the year it sat almost idle.
Buying a bigger server meant paying lakhs upfront for capacity she needed only three weeks a year.
Her IT consultant, Joseph, moved the shop to the cloud: pay for what you use, add capacity in minutes during festivals, shrink it afterwards.
'But remember,' Joseph said, 'the cloud provider secures the data centres. You still secure your passwords, your data and who has access.'

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline. Azure product names and features change often — confirm details in the official documentation.

steps.title: What is cloud computing?
steps.body:
**Cloud computing** is renting computing services — servers, storage, databases, networking, software, AI — over the internet, paying for what you use.
Key benefits:
- **High availability:** services keep running despite failures.
- **Scalability:** add resources to handle more load — **vertical** (bigger machine: more CPU/RAM) or **horizontal** (more machines).
- **Elasticity:** scaling happens automatically with demand, up and down.
- **Reliability** and **predictability** (performance and cost).
- **Security and governance** tools built in.
- **Manageability:** manage through the portal, command line, APIs and templates.

steps.title: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS — the pizza analogy
steps.body:
- **On-premises:** you make pizza at home — you own everything.
- **IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service):** you rent the kitchen. The provider runs physical hardware, network and virtualisation; you manage the operating system, patches, apps and data. Example: Azure Virtual Machines.
- **PaaS (Platform as a Service):** you order a pizza base and add toppings. The provider also manages the OS and runtime; you manage your app and data. Examples: Azure App Service, Azure SQL Database.
- **SaaS (Software as a Service):** pizza delivered. You just use the software and manage your data and users. Examples: Microsoft 365, Outlook.com.
**Serverless** (e.g. Azure Functions) is a PaaS style where you don't manage servers at all and pay per execution.

steps.title: The shared responsibility model
steps.body:
- The **provider** is always responsible for physical data centres, physical network and physical hosts.
- The **customer** is always responsible for their **information and data**, **devices** (phones, laptops) and **accounts and identities**.
- In between (OS, network controls, applications, identity infrastructure), responsibility shifts towards the provider as you move IaaS → PaaS → SaaS.

steps.title: CapEx vs OpEx, and cloud models
steps.body:
- **CapEx (capital expenditure):** big upfront spending on physical things (buying servers). Value depreciates.
- **OpEx (operational expenditure):** pay as you go for services. The cloud is mainly OpEx — the **consumption-based model**: no upfront cost, pay only for what you use, stop paying when you stop using.
Deployment models:
- **Public cloud:** services offered over the internet to anyone; no hardware to buy.
- **Private cloud:** used by one organisation, in its own data centre or hosted.
- **Hybrid cloud:** public and private connected, workloads move between them.
- **Multi-cloud:** using more than one public cloud provider. **Azure Arc** helps manage resources across on-premises, other clouds and Azure.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: List five apps or services you use (WhatsApp, a company payroll site, a VM in a lab, Gmail, a website on App Service) and label each IaaS, PaaS or SaaS. Then, for one of them, write who patches the operating system.

activity.prompt: Who is responsible? Sort each task for a company running an app on Azure Virtual Machines (IaaS).

items.text: Physical security of the data centre
Patching the VM's guest operating system
Deciding who has access to the data
Configuring firewall rules for the app

quiz.q: A company wants to stop buying servers upfront and pay monthly for what it uses. This is a shift from…
quiz.why: Buying servers upfront is capital expenditure (CapEx), while paying monthly for what you use is operating expenditure (OpEx). So this is a shift from CapEx to OpEx.

quiz.q: Which is always the customer's responsibility in every cloud model?
quiz.why: In every cloud model, the customer is always responsible for their data, accounts and identities. The provider handles physical hosts and data-centre power.

quiz.q: Azure App Service is an example of…
quiz.why: Azure App Service is PaaS: you deploy code, and Azure manages the OS and runtime.

quiz.q: Automatically adding and removing capacity as demand changes is…
quiz.why: Elasticity means capacity is added or removed automatically as demand changes.

quiz.q: Adding more VMs to share load is…
quiz.why: Adding more VMs to share load is horizontal scaling (scale out). Vertical scaling makes one VM bigger.

lessons.title: Azure architecture: regions, zones and the resource hierarchy

story.title: Where should the school portal live?

scenes.text: Imran is IT head for a group of 40 schools across India. He is moving the student portal to Azure and must decide where it runs and how to organise it.
He picks a region in India so data stays close to students and parents, and spreads servers across availability zones so one data-centre failure won't take the portal down.
He creates management groups for 'Production' and 'Non-production', separate subscriptions for each, and resource groups per application. Policies applied at the top flow down to everything.

steps.title: Regions and availability zones
steps.body:
- A **region** is a geographical area containing one or more data centres connected by a low-latency network (e.g. Central India, South India, West Europe). Choose regions for latency, data-residency rules, service availability and price.
- **Availability zones** are physically separate locations *within* a region, each with independent power, cooling and networking. Regions that support zones have at least three. Deploying across zones protects against a data-centre-level failure.
- **Zonal** services are pinned to a zone (e.g. a VM); **zone-redundant** services replicate across zones automatically (e.g. zone-redundant storage).

steps.title: Region pairs and sovereign regions
steps.body:
- Many regions are paired with another region in the same geography, typically hundreds of kilometres apart. Some services use the pair for geo-replication, and platform updates are rolled out to one region of a pair at a time. Not every region has a pair.
- **Sovereign regions** are isolated instances for compliance, such as US government regions and the Azure China regions operated by a local partner.

steps.title: The resource hierarchy
steps.body:
From top to bottom:
- **Management groups:** organise subscriptions; policies and access set here are inherited. (They can be nested several levels deep under a root management group.)
- **Subscriptions:** a billing and access boundary. Use separate subscriptions for environments, departments or billing needs.
- **Resource groups:** logical containers for resources that share a lifecycle. Each resource belongs to exactly one resource group; resource groups cannot be nested. Deleting a resource group deletes everything in it.
- **Resources:** VMs, storage accounts, databases, virtual networks…
All management goes through **Azure Resource Manager (ARM)**, whether you use the portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs or templates (ARM JSON / Bicep).

steps.title: Worked example: designing Imran's layout
steps.body:
- Root management group → 'Schools' → 'Production' and 'Non-production' management groups.
- Subscriptions: 'Schools-Prod' and 'Schools-Dev'.
- Resource groups in Prod: rg-portal-prod (web app, database), rg-network-prod (virtual network, firewall), rg-monitor-prod (Log Analytics).
- An Azure Policy at 'Production' says 'only Indian regions allowed' — automatically inherited by every subscription and resource group below.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a resource group's location limits where its resources live — it only stores the group's metadata; resources can be in other regions.
- Assuming availability zones exist in every region — check.
- Putting production and test in one resource group, so one 'delete' removes both.
- Confusing availability zones (inside one region) with region pairs (two regions).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draw the hierarchy for a company with HR, Finance and Engineering departments, each with production and test environments. Where would you apply a 'no public IPs' policy so it covers everything?

activity.prompt: Match each Azure concept to its description.
pairs: Geographical area with one or more data centres
Physically separate location within a region
Two regions in the same geography used for disaster recovery
Container for resources sharing a lifecycle

quiz.q: You need protection against a single data-centre failure within one region. Use…
quiz.why: Availability zones are separate data-centre locations within a region. Spreading across them protects you from the failure of a single data centre.

quiz.q: Can resource groups be nested inside each other?
quiz.why: Resources → resource groups → subscriptions → management groups; RGs cannot nest.
A resource group holds related resources with a shared lifecycle. Deleting it deletes all the resources inside it.

quiz.q: A policy is assigned at a management group. It applies to…
options: All subscriptions, resource groups and resources beneath it
quiz.why: Policy assigned at a management group is inherited downwards. It applies to all subscriptions, resource groups and resources beneath it.

quiz.q: Which service processes all management requests from portal, CLI and templates?
quiz.why: Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the management layer that processes all requests from the portal, CLI and templates.

lessons.title: Core services: compute, networking, storage and identity

scenes.text: A hospital chain in Bengaluru asked consultant Ananya to move its appointment system to Azure.

The old Windows app moved first to virtual machines. The new patient website went to App Service. Reports and scans went into Blob Storage. Staff sign-in moved to Microsoft Entra ID with multi-factor authentication.
A VPN connected the hospital's on-premises lab system to the Azure virtual network so both could talk securely.

steps.title: Compute
steps.body:
- **Virtual Machines (IaaS):** full control of the OS; good for lift-and-shift and custom software.
- **Virtual Machine Scale Sets:** groups of identical VMs that scale automatically.
- **Azure Virtual Desktop:** Windows desktops and apps delivered from the cloud.
- **Containers:** Azure Container Instances (run a container quickly), Azure Container Apps (serverless containers), **Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)** (managed Kubernetes for orchestrating many containers).
- **Azure App Service (PaaS):** host web apps and APIs without managing servers.
- **Azure Functions (serverless):** event-driven code that runs on demand.

steps.title: Networking
steps.body:
- **Virtual network (VNet):** your private network in Azure, divided into subnets.
- **VNet peering:** connect VNets privately (same or different regions).
- **VPN Gateway:** encrypted tunnels over the internet to on-premises (site-to-site) or individual devices (point-to-site).
- **ExpressRoute:** a private, dedicated connection from on-premises to Azure via a connectivity provider — it does not travel over the public internet.
- **Azure DNS:** host DNS domains in Azure.
- **Public and private endpoints:** private endpoints give a PaaS service a private IP inside your VNet.

steps.title: Storage
steps.body:
A **storage account** provides:
- **Blob storage:** objects such as images, videos, backups, logs.
- **Azure Files:** managed file shares (SMB/NFS).
- **Queue storage:** messages between app components.
- **Table storage:** simple NoSQL key–attribute data.
**Redundancy:** LRS (copies in one data centre), ZRS (across zones), GRS/GZRS (also copied to a secondary region), with read-access variants.
**Access tiers** for blobs: Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive — lower storage price, higher access cost and latency as you go down.
Migration tools: **Azure Migrate** (assess and migrate servers), **Azure Data Box** (physical devices for moving large data offline), **AzCopy** and **Azure Storage Explorer**.

steps.title: Identity and security
steps.body:
- **Microsoft Entra ID** (formerly Azure Active Directory): cloud identity — users, groups, sign-in, single sign-on (SSO).
- **Multi-factor authentication (MFA):** something you know + have + are.
