- **Conditional Access:** sign-in rules based on user, location, device and risk (e.g. 'require MFA outside the office').
- **Passwordless** options: Windows Hello, authenticator apps, FIDO2 keys.
- **Zero Trust:** verify explicitly, use least privilege, assume breach.
- **Defence in depth:** layers — physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application, data.
- **Microsoft Defender for Cloud:** security posture management and threat protection across Azure, hybrid and other clouds.

steps.title: How to pick a compute service
steps.body:
- Need full OS control or legacy software? **VM**.
- Web app or API, minimal ops? **App Service**.
- Small code reacting to events, pay per run? **Functions**.
- Many microservices in containers? **AKS** or **Container Apps**.
- One container, quickly, no orchestration? **Container Instances**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For Ananya's hospital, choose a service for: a nightly PDF report generator, a legacy billing app that needs Windows Server, scanned X-ray images kept for years, and doctors' sign-in. Write your reasons.

activity.prompt: Match each need to the Azure service.
pairs: Run a legacy app needing full OS control
Host a web API without managing servers
Run code when a file is uploaded, pay per execution
Private dedicated link from office to Azure, not over the internet
Store millions of images and videos

quiz.q: Which connection does NOT go over the public internet?
quiz.why: ExpressRoute is a private connection through a provider and does not use the public internet. VPNs and public endpoints go over the internet.

quiz.q: Cheapest blob tier for data rarely read and acceptable to wait hours to retrieve?
quiz.why: The Archive tier is the cheapest and is offline: reading needs rehydration, which can take hours. Hot is the most expensive to store.

quiz.q: Requiring MFA when users sign in from outside India is done with…
quiz.why: Conditional Access evaluates sign-in conditions, like location, and can require MFA. Azure Policy governs resources, not sign-ins.

quiz.q: 'Verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach' describes…
quiz.why: 'Verify explicitly, use least privilege, assume breach' are the principles of Zero Trust.

quiz.q: Moving 80 TB of archives to Azure when the internet link is slow — consider…
quiz.why: Azure Data Box ships physical storage devices, so large data like 80 TB can be moved when the internet link is slow.

lessons.title: Management and governance: cost, policy, compliance and monitoring

scenes.text: A start-up in Gurugram got an Azure bill three times higher than expected. Intern Harsh had left 20 large test VMs running over a long weekend.
CTO Farah opened Cost Management, found the cost by resource group and tag, and set budgets with alerts at 80% and 100%.
She added an Azure Policy allowing only small VM sizes in the dev subscription, a delete lock on production, and tags for 'owner' and 'environment'. The next month's bill matched the forecast.

steps.title: What affects cost, and the tools
steps.body:
Cost factors: resource type and size, consumption, region, **bandwidth** (data leaving Azure regions is generally charged), reservations and savings plans, licences you already own (**Azure Hybrid Benefit** for eligible Windows Server/SQL Server licences), and Spot VMs for interruptible work.
Tools:
- **Pricing calculator:** estimate the cost of a planned solution before building.
- **Microsoft Cost Management:** analyse actual spending, create **budgets** and **alerts**, view recommendations.
- **Tags:** name–value labels (owner=farah, env=dev, costcentre=1042) to group costs and manage resources.

steps.title: Governance tools
steps.body:
- **Azure Policy:** create rules that resources must follow (allowed regions, allowed VM sizes, required tags); can deny non-compliant deployments, audit them, or remediate. Groups of policies are **initiatives**.
- **Resource locks:** prevent accidental changes — **Delete** (CanNotDelete: can modify, can't delete) or **Read-only** (can't modify or delete). Locks apply even to owners until removed.
- **Microsoft Purview:** data governance, discovery, classification and compliance across data estates.
- **Service Trust Portal:** Microsoft's compliance reports and documentation.

steps.title: Monitoring and SLAs
steps.body:
- **Azure Advisor:** personalised recommendations on reliability, security, performance, cost and operational excellence.
- **Azure Service Health:** status of Azure services and regions affecting *you* — outages, planned maintenance, health advisories.
- **Azure Monitor:** collect and analyse metrics and logs; **Log Analytics** for queries; **alerts**; **Application Insights** for application performance.
- **SLA (service-level agreement):** Microsoft's uptime commitment for a service (e.g. 99.9%, 99.99%), with service credits if missed. Higher SLAs usually need redundant designs. Combining dependent services lowers the composite SLA (multiply them: 99.9% × 99.9% ≈ 99.8%).

steps.title: Worked example: what does 99.9% allow?
steps.body:
A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes.
- 99.9% → 0.1% downtime ≈ 43 minutes a month.
- 99.95% → ≈ 21.6 minutes.
- 99.99% → ≈ 4.3 minutes.
If your app needs a web tier (99.95%) AND a database (99.99%), the composite is 0.9995 × 0.9999 ≈ 99.94%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a budget *stops* spending — budgets alert; they do not automatically shut resources down (you can trigger automation from alerts).
- Confusing **Azure Policy** (what resources can be/how configured) with **RBAC** (who can do what).
- Assuming tags are inherited by resources from resource groups — not by default (Policy can enforce it).
- Confusing Service Health (Azure's status for you) with Azure Monitor (your resources' telemetry).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write three Azure Policies, two tags and one budget alert you would set up on day one for a student project subscription. Explain each in one line.

a.text: You are Farah. Developers keep creating huge VMs in the dev subscription. What is the best preventive control?

choices.label: Azure Policy: allowed VM sizes, effect Deny
A budget alert
choices.feedback: Budgets notify after spending happens; they do not prevent large VMs.

choices.label: Give everyone the Reader role
choices.feedback: That stops all work, not just big VMs.

b.text: Next, someone almost deleted the production database. How do you prevent accidental deletion while still allowing changes?

choices.label: Apply a Read-only lock
choices.feedback: Read-only also blocks legitimate changes and can break some operations.

c.text: You get an alert at 80% of budget — but the large VMs are already running.

choices.label: Add a Deny policy for VM sizes
choices.feedback: Prevention plus alerts is the right combination.

c2.text: Developers can no longer deploy anything. Work stops.

choices.label: Restore Contributor and use Policy for VM sizes
choices.feedback: RBAC controls who; Policy controls what.

c3.text: The database team can't apply a needed configuration change.

d.text: Policy prevents oversized VMs, a Delete lock protects production, budgets alert on spending and tags show who owns what. That is governance in practice.

quiz.q: Estimate the monthly cost of a solution before deploying it — use…
quiz.why: The Azure pricing calculator estimates the monthly cost of planned resources before deployment. Cost Management analyses spending that has already happened.

quiz.q: Which lock allows changes but blocks deletion?
quiz.why: A CanNotDelete lock allows changes but blocks deletion. A ReadOnly lock blocks changes as well.

quiz.q: Which service tells you about an Azure outage affecting your region?
quiz.why: Azure Service Health gives personalised information about Azure outages and issues that affect your services and regions.

quiz.q: Composite SLA of two required services at 99.9% each?
quiz.why: For services that are both required, multiply their SLAs: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.998, or about 99.8%. The combined SLA is lower than either one.

quiz.q: Ensure every resource has a 'costcentre' tag — use…
quiz.why: Azure Policy can require a tag or add it automatically, so every resource gets a 'costcentre' tag.

questions.q: Which model gives you the most control over the operating system?
questions.why: IaaS gives the most control: you manage the operating system and everything above it. PaaS and SaaS leave more to the provider.
Microsoft 365 is SaaS: complete software delivered as a service.

questions.q: What is the main billing boundary in Azure?
questions.why: The subscription is the main billing boundary in Azure. Resources in a subscription are billed together.

questions.q: Which tool gives recommendations to reduce cost and improve reliability?
questions.why: Azure Advisor gives personalised recommendations to reduce cost and improve reliability, security and performance.

questions.q: Physical security of Azure data centres is the responsibility of…
questions.why: Physical security of data centres is always the provider's responsibility, so Microsoft handles it for Azure.

questions.q: A company runs workloads both in its data centre and in Azure, connected together. This is…
questions.why: Running workloads both in your own data centre and in Azure, connected together, is a hybrid cloud.

questions.q: You must manage on-premises servers and servers in another cloud from Azure. Use…
questions.why: Azure Arc extends Azure management to on-premises servers and other clouds.

questions.q: A web app must stay available if one data centre in the region fails. Deploy across…
questions.why: Availability zones are separate data centres within a region. Deploying across them keeps the app up if one data centre fails.

questions.q: Which statement about resource groups is true?
options: A resource belongs to exactly one resource group
Resources in a group must be in the group's region
Resources can belong to many groups
questions.why: A resource belongs to exactly one resource group. Groups cannot be nested, and resources in a group can be in different regions.

questions.q: Users must sign in with MFA only when connecting from unknown locations. Which feature?
questions.why: Conditional Access can require MFA only in certain conditions, like unknown locations. RBAC and locks do not check sign-in conditions.

questions.q: A budget alert fires at 100%. What happens to running resources by default?
options: They keep running; the budget only notifies
questions.why: A budget only sends alerts; it does not stop anything by default. Running resources keep running unless you add automation.

questions.q: You have eligible on-premises Windows Server licences and want lower VM costs. Use…
questions.why: Azure Hybrid Benefit lets you reuse eligible on-premises Windows Server licences on Azure VMs to cut cost.

questions.q: 99.99% monthly availability allows roughly how much downtime in a 30-day month?
questions.why: A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes. Allowed downtime at 99.99% is 0.01% of that, which is about 4.3 minutes.

questions.q: Data classification and discovery across your data estate is the job of…
questions.why: Microsoft Purview handles data governance, including discovering and classifying data across your data estate.

questions.q: A web tier (99.95%) depends on a database (99.99%). Approximate composite SLA?
questions.why: For dependent services, multiply the SLAs: 0.9995 × 0.9999 ≈ 0.9994, or about 99.94%. This is lower than either alone.

courses.title: Azure administrator I: identities, governance and storage (AZ-104 style)
courses.summary: For engineers preparing for the administrator exam: Microsoft Entra users and groups, role-based access control, Azure Policy, locks, tags and subscriptions, storage accounts, redundancy, tiers, secure access and Azure Files — with scenario questions. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can manage Entra users, groups, guest access, licences and self-service password reset
Learners can assign RBAC roles at the right scope and interpret effective permissions
Learners can apply Azure Policy, locks, tags and cost controls and move resources safely
Learners can configure storage accounts with suitable redundancy, tiers and lifecycle rules
Learners can secure storage with Entra authorisation, SAS, keys, firewalls and private endpoints, and configure Azure Files and File Sync

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra ID: users, groups and access

scenes.text: Sandeep is the Azure administrator at an IT services company in Pune. 300 freshers join on Monday across five departments.
Creating users one by one would take days. He bulk-creates them from a CSV and uses dynamic groups: anyone with department = 'Finance' automatically lands in the Finance group.
An external auditor from a partner firm needs temporary access. Sandeep invites her as a guest instead of creating a new internal account.
He enables self-service password reset, so forgotten passwords no longer flood the helpdesk.

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline. Practise every task hands-on in a free or sandbox subscription — the administrator exam rewards real experience.

steps.title: Users
steps.body:
- **Cloud users** are created in Microsoft Entra ID; **synchronised users** come from on-premises Active Directory via Microsoft Entra Connect (Sync or Cloud Sync).
- **Guest users** are external people invited through **B2B collaboration**; they sign in with their own organisation's or personal account.
- Bulk operations: create, invite or delete users from a CSV in the portal, or script with PowerShell / Microsoft Graph.
- Properties such as department, job title and usage location matter: usage location is required before assigning many licences, and attributes drive dynamic groups.

steps.title: Groups
steps.body:
- **Group types:** **Security** groups (grant access to resources) and **Microsoft 365** groups (shared mailbox, calendar, files for collaboration).
- **Membership types:**
  - **Assigned:** members added manually.
  - **Dynamic user / dynamic device:** membership calculated from rules, e.g. (user.department -eq "Finance"). Dynamic groups require a Microsoft Entra ID P1 (or higher) licence.
- Assign roles and licences to groups rather than individuals — easier to manage and audit.
- **Administrative units** let you delegate admin rights over a subset of users (e.g. the Mumbai office helpdesk).

steps.title: Licences, SSPR and sign-in security
steps.body:
- **Editions:** Free, P1, P2 (P2 adds features such as Identity Protection and Privileged Identity Management). Features like Conditional Access and dynamic groups need P1 or higher.
- **Group-based licensing** assigns licences automatically to group members.
- **Self-service password reset (SSPR):** can be enabled for none, selected groups, or all users; choose the number of methods required (one or two) and which methods are allowed (authenticator app, SMS, email, security questions etc.).
- **Device identities:** Entra registered (personal devices), Entra joined (organisation-owned, cloud), hybrid joined (on-premises AD plus Entra).

steps.title: Two different role systems
steps.body:
- **Microsoft Entra roles** control the *directory*: Global Administrator, User Administrator, Helpdesk Administrator, etc.
- **Azure RBAC roles** control *Azure resources*: Owner, Contributor, Reader… (next lesson).
A Global Administrator doesn't automatically manage Azure subscriptions, but can elevate their access to gain User Access Administrator at the root scope when needed.

steps.title: Worked example: a dynamic group rule
steps.body:
Requirement: all full-time employees in Sales in India.
Rule: (user.department -eq "Sales") -and (user.country -eq "India") -and (user.employeeType -eq "FTE")
Then assign the Sales security group to the CRM app and a licence through group-based licensing. When HR updates a person's department, membership updates automatically (processing can take some time).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In a test tenant: create a user, a guest invitation, an assigned security group and (if you have a trial P1 licence) a dynamic group. Enable SSPR for one pilot group with two required methods.

a.text: You are Sandeep. HR wants every new Finance hire to get Finance resources automatically, with no tickets. What do you configure?

choices.label: A dynamic security group with rule user.department -eq Finance
choices.feedback: Correct — membership follows the attribute. Remember the P1 licence requirement.

choices.label: An assigned group and ask HR to email you each hire
choices.feedback: Works, but manual and error-prone — not what was asked.

b.text: The dynamic group option is greyed out in the portal. Most likely reason?

choices.label: The tenant lacks a Microsoft Entra ID P1 (or higher) licence
choices.feedback: Yes — dynamic membership requires P1 or above.

choices.label: Dynamic groups only work for guests
choices.feedback: No — dynamic rules work for users and devices.

c.text: Two hires were missed in week one and couldn't open their reports.

c2.text: You check the documentation: dynamic membership is a licensed feature.

d.text: With P1 in place, the dynamic group fills itself, group-based licensing assigns licences, and SSPR handles password resets. Onboarding is now hands-off.

quiz.q: An external consultant needs access using her own company account. Best approach?
options: Invite her as a B2B guest user
quiz.why: Guest (B2B) users sign in with their own company identity, so you do not manage her password. Sharing an admin password or creating an internal user is poor practice.

quiz.q: Which licence is needed for dynamic group membership?
options: Microsoft Entra ID P1 or higher
quiz.why: Dynamic group membership needs Microsoft Entra ID P1 or higher. The free tier does not support it.

quiz.q: Which group type gives a shared mailbox and calendar?
quiz.why: A Microsoft 365 group is for collaboration and gives a shared mailbox, calendar and files. A security group is for access control.

quiz.q: You want the Delhi helpdesk to reset passwords only for Delhi users. Use…
options: Administrative units with a scoped role
quiz.why: Administrative units scope directory roles to a subset of users. A helpdesk admin can then reset passwords only for the Delhi users.

quiz.q: Before assigning a licence to a user, which property is commonly required?
quiz.why: Licensing depends on the user's usage location (country), so it must be set before a licence can be assigned.

story.title: The contractor who could see everything

scenes.text: A contractor, Ben, was hired to fix one web app. Someone gave him Contributor on the whole subscription 'to save time'.
During an audit, Meera, the cloud security lead in Hyderabad, found Ben could modify the production database and networking too.
She removed the subscription-level assignment and gave him Website Contributor on just the app's resource group, for the length of the contract. Least privilege restored.

steps.title: The three parts of a role assignment
steps.body:
A role assignment = **security principal** + **role definition** + **scope**.
- **Principal:** a user, group, service principal, or managed identity.
- **Role definition:** a set of allowed actions (Actions, NotActions, DataActions, NotDataActions).
- **Scope:** management group → subscription → resource group → resource. Assignments are **inherited** by everything below the scope.

steps.title: Key built-in roles
steps.body:
- **Owner:** full access to resources, including assigning roles to others.
- **Contributor:** full access to manage resources, but cannot assign roles or change access.
- **Reader:** view everything, change nothing.
- **User Access Administrator:** manage access (role assignments) only.
- **Role Based Access Control Administrator:** manage role assignments, optionally with conditions limiting which roles can be assigned.
- Plus many service-specific roles: Virtual Machine Contributor, Network Contributor, Storage Blob Data Reader/Contributor, Website Contributor, etc.
**Control plane vs data plane:** Contributor on a storage account can manage the account but reading blob *data* with Entra authorisation needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader.

steps.title: Effective permissions
steps.body:
- Permissions are **additive**: a user's effective access is the union of all role assignments from all their groups and scopes.
- NotActions just exclude actions from that role; they are *not* a deny. Another role can still grant the action.
- **Deny assignments** block actions even if a role grants them; they are created by Azure in specific cases (for example, managed applications) rather than by you directly.
- Use **Check access** in the portal (Access control (IAM)) to see a principal's assignments.

steps.title: Worked example: a custom role
steps.body:
Requirement: operators can start, restart and deallocate VMs, but not create or delete them.
Custom role (JSON outline):
- Actions: Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/read, …/start/action, …/restart/action, …/deallocate/action
- NotActions: none
- AssignableScopes: /subscriptions/<id>/resourceGroups/rg-app-prod
Assign it to the 'VM Operators' group at the resource group scope.

steps.title: Common exam and real-life traps
steps.body:
- Contributor **cannot** grant access to others; Owner or User Access Administrator can.
- Assigning at subscription scope when only one resource group was needed.
- Assigning roles to individuals instead of groups.
- Forgetting that a Reader at a higher scope can see resources below even if not granted directly.
- For time-bound admin access, use **Privileged Identity Management** (P2) — just-in-time, approval, expiry.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In a sandbox: assign Reader to a test user at a resource group, sign in as that user and try to create a resource. Then add a Virtual Machine Contributor assignment and observe what changes. Use Check access to confirm.

activity.prompt: Match each requirement to the least-privilege built-in role.
pairs: Manage all resources but not grant access
Read blob data with Entra authorisation
Manage VMs but not the VNet they connect to

quiz.q: A user has Reader at subscription and Contributor on rg-web. On rg-web they can…
quiz.why: Azure role permissions are additive. Reader at the subscription plus Contributor on rg-web means the user can manage resources in rg-web.

quiz.q: Who can assign Azure roles to others?
quiz.why: Only Owner or User Access Administrator can assign Azure roles. Contributor can manage resources but cannot grant access.

options: Exclude actions from that role only
quiz.why: NotActions exclude actions from that one role only. They are not a deny, so another role can still grant them.

quiz.q: An admin needs Owner for 2 hours with approval. Use…
quiz.why: Privileged Identity Management (PIM) gives just-in-time, time-bound, approved access, such as Owner for 2 hours.

quiz.q: Contributor on a storage account but 'authorisation failed' when reading blobs with Entra sign-in. Why?
options: A data role like Storage Blob Data Reader is required
quiz.why: Contributor is a control-plane role and does not give data access. Reading blobs with Entra sign-in needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader.

lessons.title: Governance: Policy, locks, tags, subscriptions and cost

scenes.text: An external auditor found that a bank's test team had created storage accounts outside India and without the required encryption settings.
Cloud governance lead Priya created an initiative of policies — allowed locations, required tags, secure transfer required — and assigned it at the management group.
The compliance dashboard showed 37 existing non-compliant resources. She used remediation tasks to fix what could be fixed automatically and opened tickets for the rest.

steps.title: Azure Policy in depth
steps.body:
- **Policy definition:** a rule (JSON) with a condition and an **effect**.
- **Initiative:** a group of definitions assigned together.
- **Assignment:** applies a definition/initiative at a scope; you can exclude child scopes, and create **exemptions**.
Common effects:
- **Deny:** block non-compliant create/update requests.
- **Audit:** allow but mark non-compliant.
- **Append / Modify:** add or change properties (e.g. add a tag).
- **AuditIfNotExists / DeployIfNotExists:** check for, or deploy, a related resource (e.g. a diagnostic setting).
- **Disabled.**
Existing resources are evaluated for compliance; Modify and DeployIfNotExists can fix them with **remediation tasks** (which use a managed identity).

steps.title: Locks
steps.body:
- **CanNotDelete (Delete):** read and modify allowed, delete blocked.
- **ReadOnly:** read only; modify and delete blocked.
- Inherited by child resources; the most restrictive lock wins.
- Locks apply to everyone, including Owners — remove the lock first (needs permission on Microsoft.Authorization/locks).
- Gotcha: a ReadOnly lock can break operations that use POST requests, such as listing storage account keys.

steps.title: Tags, subscriptions and moving resources
steps.body:
- **Tags:** name–value pairs; resources do not inherit tags from resource groups by default — use Policy (Modify/Append, e.g. 'Inherit a tag from the resource group') to enforce.
- **Subscriptions** can be organised under management groups; you can transfer billing ownership and move subscriptions between management groups.
- **Moving resources** between resource groups or subscriptions: not every resource type supports moves; dependent resources may need moving together; during a move both source and target resource groups are locked for write and delete operations (the resources keep running). Validate first.

steps.title: Cost management for admins
steps.body:
- **Budgets** at subscription or resource-group scope, with alerts to action groups (which can trigger automation).
- **Cost analysis** by tag, resource group, service, location.
- **Azure Advisor** cost recommendations (resize or shut down idle VMs, buy reservations).
- **Reservations / savings plans** for steady workloads; **Spot VMs** for interruptible jobs; auto-shutdown schedules for dev VMs.

steps.title: Worked example: choosing the effect
steps.body:
- 'No resources outside Central India and South India' → Allowed locations, **Deny**.
- 'We want to know which VMs lack backup, but not block deployments' → **AuditIfNotExists**.
- 'Every resource must get the env tag from its resource group' → **Modify** (with remediation for existing resources).
- 'Every new key vault must send diagnostic logs to Log Analytics' → **DeployIfNotExists**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In a sandbox, assign the built-in 'Allowed locations' policy to a resource group with Deny, then try creating a storage account in another region. Read the error message — you will see it on the exam and at work.

activity.prompt: Pick the best Azure Policy effect for each requirement.

items.text: Block VMs larger than D4s sizes in dev
Report storage accounts that allow public blob access, without blocking yet
Automatically add a costcentre tag copied from the resource group
Automatically create diagnostic settings on new SQL servers
Find VMs without the monitoring agent

quiz.q: You assign a Deny policy. What happens to existing non-compliant resources?
options: They are marked non-compliant but keep running
quiz.why: A Deny policy blocks new or updated non-compliant resources. Existing ones are only reported as non-compliant and keep running.

quiz.q: Which effect can fix existing resources through a remediation task?
quiz.why: Remediation tasks can fix existing resources for policies with Modify or DeployIfNotExists effects. Audit and Deny cannot change anything.

quiz.q: A ReadOnly lock on a storage account may stop…
options: Reading blobs via the portal entirely in all cases
quiz.why: A ReadOnly lock blocks operations like listing account keys, since that is a POST request. Viewing properties is still possible.

quiz.q: Are tags inherited from resource groups by default?
quiz.why: Tags are not inherited from resource groups by default. You can use Azure Policy to make resources inherit them.

quiz.q: While resources move between resource groups…
options: Source and target groups are locked for writes/deletes until the move completes
quiz.why: While resources are being moved, the source and target resource groups are locked for writes and deletes until the move finishes. The resources keep running.

lessons.title: Storage accounts: redundancy, tiers and data protection

scenes.text: A logistics firm must keep warehouse CCTV footage: the last 30 days readily available, and up to several years for legal disputes.
Administrator Naveen calculated that keeping everything in the Hot tier would be very expensive.
He set a lifecycle rule: move blobs to Cool after 30 days, to Archive after 180 days, delete after the retention period. He chose geo-redundant storage so a regional disaster wouldn't lose evidence.

steps.title: Storage account basics
steps.body:
- Name: 3–24 characters, lowercase letters and numbers only, **globally unique** (it becomes part of the URL, e.g. https://name.blob.core.windows.net).
- **Standard general-purpose v2** is the usual choice (blobs, files, queues, tables).
- **Premium** types for low latency: premium block blobs, premium file shares, premium page blobs.
- **Secure transfer required** (HTTPS only) is on by default; set a minimum TLS version.

steps.title: Redundancy options
steps.body:
- **LRS:** three copies within a single data centre in the primary region. Cheapest; doesn't protect against a data-centre or regional disaster.
- **ZRS:** three copies across availability zones in the primary region.
- **GRS:** LRS in the primary + asynchronous copy to the paired secondary region (LRS there).
- **GZRS:** ZRS in the primary + copy to the secondary region.
- **RA-GRS / RA-GZRS:** as above, plus **read access** to the secondary endpoint at any time.
With GRS/GZRS (without RA), the secondary is readable only after a failover. Customer-managed failover is available for many account types. Premium accounts support only LRS and (for some types) ZRS.

steps.title: Access tiers and lifecycle management
steps.body:
- **Hot:** frequently accessed; highest storage cost, lowest access cost.
- **Cool:** infrequent; minimum 30 days (early-deletion charge if moved/deleted sooner).
- **Cold:** rarely accessed; minimum 90 days.
- **Archive:** offline, cheapest storage; minimum 180 days; blobs must be **rehydrated** to an online tier before reading, which can take hours (high priority is faster for smaller blobs).
Archive is set per blob (block blobs). **Lifecycle management** rules move or delete blobs based on age (last modified / last accessed / creation) and filters (prefix, blob index tags).

steps.title: Data protection features
steps.body:
- **Soft delete** for blobs and containers (recover deleted items within a retention period).
- **Blob versioning** (keeps previous versions automatically).
- **Point-in-time restore** for block blobs (needs versioning, change feed and soft delete).
- **Immutable storage** (time-based retention or legal hold — WORM, write once read many) for compliance evidence.
- **Object replication:** asynchronously copy block blobs between accounts (requires versioning on both and change feed on the source).
- Tools: **AzCopy** (fast command-line copy), **Azure Storage Explorer** (GUI), **Azure Import/Export** and **Data Box** for offline transfer.

steps.title: Worked example: Naveen's lifecycle rule (logic)
steps.body:
Filter: container 'cctv', prefix 'warehouse/'.
- If days since last modified > 30 → tier to Cool.
- If days since last modified > 180 → tier to Archive.
- If days since last modified > retention limit → delete.
Plus: immutability policy with legal hold on footage involved in an active dispute, so even admins cannot delete it.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Create a GPv2 account, upload a file, change its tier to Cool, then Archive, then try to download it — note the error. Start a rehydration and note how long it takes.

a.text: A bank needs storage that survives a full region outage AND lets its reporting app read data from the secondary region at any time. Which redundancy?

choices.label: RA-GRS or RA-GZRS
choices.feedback: Correct — geo-replication plus read access to the secondary.

choices.label: ZRS
choices.feedback: ZRS stays within one region; a regional outage would still hit it.

choices.label: GRS
choices.feedback: GRS replicates, but the secondary is readable only after failover.

b.text: Logs older than 90 days are read maybe once a year, and a few hours' delay is acceptable. Cheapest approach?

choices.label: Lifecycle rule to Archive (respecting the 180-day minimum)
choices.feedback: Yes — Archive is cheapest for rarely read data where delays are fine.

choices.label: Keep everything in Hot
choices.feedback: Works, but costs far more than needed.

c.text: A regional disaster makes the data unavailable.

choices.label: Choose a geo-redundant option with read access

c2.text: The reporting app tries to read the secondary and is refused — no failover has happened.

choices.label: Upgrade to RA-GRS / RA-GZRS
choices.feedback: Read access to the secondary is what 'RA' provides.

c3.text: The finance team flags storage as the fastest-growing cost.

d.text: RA-GZRS for resilience and readable secondary, lifecycle tiering to Cool and Archive, soft delete and versioning for mistakes. A balanced, defensible design.

quiz.q: Which redundancy keeps three copies in ONE data centre?
quiz.why: LRS (locally redundant storage) keeps three copies in a single data centre. ZRS spreads across zones, and GRS adds another region.

quiz.q: Minimum storage duration for Archive tier?
quiz.why: The Archive tier has a 180-day minimum storage period. Deleting or moving a blob earlier causes an early-deletion charge.

quiz.q: A blob in Archive must be read today. First you must…
options: Rehydrate it to an online tier
quiz.why: Blobs in Archive are offline. To read one, you must rehydrate it to an online tier (Hot or Cool) first, which can take hours.

quiz.q: Which name is valid for a storage account?
quiz.why: Storage account names must be 3–24 characters, using lowercase letters and numbers only. 'contosodata2025' fits; capitals, hyphens and underscores are not allowed.

quiz.q: Compliance requires that audit files cannot be changed or deleted for 7 years. Use…
quiz.why: Immutable storage with a time-based retention policy gives WORM (write once, read many) protection. Data cannot be changed or deleted during the period.

lessons.title: Securing storage access and Azure Files

scenes.text: A design agency in Mumbai shared a link to a client folder. The link used the storage account key and never expired. Months later, an ex-employee could still read files.
Administrator Grace rotated the keys, moved apps to Microsoft Entra authorisation with managed identities, and replaced shared links with short-lived user delegation SAS tokens.
For the office's old Windows file server, she set up Azure Files with Azure File Sync, so the branch kept fast local access while the cloud held the master copy.

steps.title: Ways to authorise access
steps.body:
- **Microsoft Entra ID + RBAC (recommended):** users, groups or **managed identities** get data roles (Storage Blob Data Reader/Contributor, Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor, etc.). No secrets to leak.
- **Account access keys:** two keys giving full access to the account. Rotate regularly (use key 2 while regenerating key 1); store in Key Vault; consider disabling shared-key access entirely.
- **Shared access signatures (SAS):** time-limited, permission-limited tokens:
  - **User delegation SAS:** signed with Entra credentials (blob storage) — the most secure SAS type.
  - **Service SAS:** one service (blob, file, queue or table), signed with the account key.
  - **Account SAS:** one or more services, signed with the account key.
- **Stored access policy:** defines SAS settings on a container; revoking or changing the policy invalidates service SAS tokens linked to it — a way to revoke without rotating keys.

steps.title: Network security for storage
steps.body:
- **Storage firewall:** allow only selected virtual networks and IP ranges (default action Deny).
- **Service endpoints:** traffic from a subnet reaches storage over the Azure backbone; storage still has a public endpoint.
- **Private endpoints:** give the storage account a private IP in your VNet (with private DNS); you can disable public network access completely.
- Allow trusted Microsoft services where needed (e.g. backup).

steps.title: Azure Files and Azure File Sync
steps.body:
- **Azure Files:** fully managed shares over **SMB** (Windows, Linux, macOS) and **NFS** (Linux, premium tier). Identity-based SMB access can use on-premises AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services or Microsoft Entra Kerberos (for hybrid identities).
- **Snapshots** for point-in-time recovery of shares; soft delete for shares.
- **Azure File Sync:** caches an Azure file share on Windows Servers. Components: **Storage Sync Service** → **sync group** → one **cloud endpoint** (the Azure file share) + **server endpoints** (paths on registered servers). **Cloud tiering** keeps hot files local and moves cold files to the cloud, leaving pointers.

steps.title: Worked example: choosing access for three cases
steps.body:
- A web app on App Service reads product images → enable a **managed identity**, grant **Storage Blob Data Reader** on the container. No keys in code.
- A client must upload files for 48 hours → **user delegation SAS** with write/create only, HTTPS only, expiry 48 h, optionally IP-restricted.
- An old script uses the account key and cannot be changed this month → store key in Key Vault, plan key rotation, and track the migration to Entra auth.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- A SAS signed with an account key can't be revoked except by rotating that key (or via a stored access policy for service SAS).
- Private endpoint created but DNS not updated → clients still resolve the public IP.
- Firewall enabled and forgetting the admin's own IP → portal shows access errors on data.
- SMB uses TCP port 445; many ISPs and networks block it, so mounting Azure Files from home may fail — use VPN/ExpressRoute or File Sync.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Generate a SAS for one blob with read-only permission and a 15-minute expiry. Open it in a browser, wait for expiry and try again. Then create a stored access policy and see how changing it affects a linked SAS.

statements.s: A user delegation SAS is signed with Microsoft Entra credentials.
statements.why: It does not use the account key.

statements.s: Contributor on the storage account automatically lets a user read blobs through Entra authorisation.
A private endpoint gives the storage account a private IP address in your VNet.
statements.why: Traffic stays private; pair it with private DNS.

statements.s: An Azure File Sync sync group can have multiple cloud endpoints.
statements.why: One cloud endpoint, many server endpoints.

statements.s: Rotating the account key invalidates SAS tokens signed with that key.
SMB access to Azure Files uses port 445.

quiz.q: Most secure way for an App Service app to read blobs?
options: Managed identity with a Storage Blob Data role
quiz.why: A managed identity with a Storage Blob Data role needs no secrets. Account keys or SAS tokens can leak, and a public container exposes the data.

quiz.q: You must revoke several service SAS tokens without rotating keys. Use…
quiz.why: A stored access policy lets you revoke linked service SAS tokens by changing or deleting the policy, without rotating the account keys.

quiz.q: Branch offices need fast local access to a file share whose master copy is in Azure. Use…
quiz.why: Azure File Sync caches the Azure file share on a local Windows Server, giving branch offices fast local access.

quiz.q: After creating a private endpoint, clients still reach the public IP. Likely cause?
options: DNS still resolves to the public endpoint
quiz.why: A private endpoint only helps if DNS resolves the storage name to its private IP. If DNS still resolves to the public endpoint, configure the private DNS zone.

quiz.q: Which SAS type covers multiple services in one token?
quiz.why: An account SAS can cover multiple storage services in one token. A service SAS covers one service.

questions.q: Which role lets a user manage resources but not grant access?
questions.why: Contributor can manage resources, but cannot assign roles. Owner can do both.

questions.q: Which redundancy copies data across availability zones in one region?
questions.why: ZRS (zone-redundant storage) copies data across availability zones in one region. LRS stays in one data centre and GRS goes to another region.

questions.q: External partners should sign in with their own accounts to access an app. Use…
questions.why: Guest users via B2B collaboration let partners sign in with their own accounts. You do not have to create or manage their credentials.

questions.q: Which policy effect blocks non-compliant deployments?
questions.why: The Deny effect blocks non-compliant deployments. Audit only reports them.

questions.q: You want to prevent deletion of a production resource group but allow updates. Apply…
questions.why: A CanNotDelete lock stops deletion but still allows updates. A ReadOnly lock would block updates too.

questions.q: Scenario: User A is in Group X (Reader on subscription) and Group Y (Contributor on rg-data). Can A delete a VM in rg-data?
questions.why: Effective permissions are the union; Contributor on rg-data allows it (unless a lock or deny assignment blocks it).

questions.q: Scenario: blobs must be cheap to store, read about once a year, and retrieval within a few hours is fine. Tier?
questions.why: For data read about once a year, where retrieval in hours is fine, the Archive tier is the cheapest. Its data must be rehydrated before reading.

questions.q: Scenario: dynamic membership rules cannot be created. What should you check first?
options: Whether the tenant has Microsoft Entra ID P1 or higher
questions.why: Dynamic group membership requires Microsoft Entra ID P1 or higher. If you cannot create dynamic rules, check the tenant's licence first.

questions.q: Scenario: a script must list storage account keys, but fails with an authorisation error even though you are Owner. A lock is on the account. Which lock?
questions.why: A ReadOnly lock blocks the POST operation that lists storage account keys, even for an Owner. A CanNotDelete lock does not.

questions.q: Scenario: you need read access to the secondary region at all times, plus protection from a zone failure in the primary. Choose…
questions.why: RA-GZRS has zone-redundant storage in the primary region, a geo copy in the secondary and read access to the secondary. RA-GRS lacks the zone protection in the primary.

questions.q: Scenario: existing resources lack a required tag. You assign a Modify policy. What else is needed to fix existing resources?
questions.why: A Modify policy only acts on resources that are created or updated after assignment. To fix existing non-compliant resources, you must also run a remediation task.

questions.q: Scenario: operators must start and stop VMs in one resource group only, nothing else. Best solution?
options: Custom role with start/restart/deallocate actions, assigned at that resource group to a group
questions.why: Least privilege means giving only the needed actions at the smallest scope. A custom role with start, restart and deallocate, assigned to a group at that one resource group, does exactly that. Owner or subscription Contributor is far too broad.

questions.q: Scenario: a contractor received an account-key SAS with no expiry; you must cut access immediately, and other apps use key 2. Best action?
options: Regenerate key 1 (the key used to sign the SAS)
questions.why: A SAS from an account key is signed with that key. Regenerating key 1 invalidates the SAS tokens signed with it, while apps using key 2 keep working.

questions.q: Scenario: Azure File Sync — you add a second Windows Server in another branch to the same sync group. What do you create?
options: A new server endpoint on the registered server
A new Storage Sync Service per server
questions.why: A sync group has one cloud endpoint (the Azure file share) and can have many server endpoints. For the new server, register it and create a new server endpoint on it.

courses.title: Azure administrator II: compute, networking, monitoring and backup (AZ-104 style)
courses.summary: For mid-senior engineers preparing for the administrator exam: virtual machines and availability, templates, App Service and containers, virtual networks, NSGs, peering, load balancing, DNS and hybrid connectivity, Azure Monitor and backup/recovery — with scenario questions. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can deploy and manage VMs, disks, availability sets/zones and scale sets, including with ARM/Bicep templates
Learners can configure App Service plans, deployment slots and container services
Learners can design VNets and subnets, NSGs/ASGs, peering, routes and private access
Learners can choose between Load Balancer, Application Gateway and other traffic services and configure DNS and hybrid links
Learners can monitor with metrics, logs, KQL and alerts, and protect workloads with Azure Backup and Site Recovery

story.title: The patch night that took the site down

scenes.text: A travel booking company in Jaipur ran its web tier on two VMs. During a platform maintenance event both VMs rebooted together — the site was down for 20 minutes during peak booking.
Cloud engineer Vikram found the VMs were not in an availability set or across zones, so nothing stopped them sharing the same hardware and update schedule.
He redeployed with a Bicep template: VMs across availability zones behind a load balancer, managed disks, and a scale set for peak season.

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline. SLA numbers and feature details change — always verify in current documentation.

steps.title: VM essentials
steps.body:
- **Size families** (general purpose, compute, memory, storage, GPU). Resizing restarts the VM; if the new size isn't available on the current hardware cluster you must **deallocate** first.
- **Stopped vs deallocated:** shutting down inside the OS leaves the VM allocated (compute still billed). **Stop (deallocate)** from Azure releases compute (disks still billed).
- **Managed disks:** Standard HDD, Standard SSD, Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2, Ultra Disk. Data is encrypted at rest by default (server-side encryption with platform-managed keys); options include customer-managed keys, **encryption at host**, and **Azure Disk Encryption** (BitLocker/DM-Crypt inside the guest).
- Connect securely with **Azure Bastion** (RDP/SSH through the browser, no public IP on the VM) or just-in-time VM access.

steps.title: Availability options
steps.body:
- **Availability set:** spreads VMs across **fault domains** (separate racks/power — up to 3) and **update domains** (rebooted at different times during planned maintenance — up to 20, default 5). Protects against hardware failure and maintenance within a data centre.
- **Availability zones:** VMs in separate data centres within a region — protects against a data-centre failure.
- **Virtual Machine Scale Sets:** identical (or flexible) VMs with **autoscale** rules (e.g. add 2 instances when average CPU > 70% for 10 minutes).
Indicative VM SLAs (check current terms): two or more VMs across zones 99.99%; in an availability set 99.95%; a single VM with Premium SSD/Ultra disks 99.9%.

steps.title: ARM templates and Bicep
steps.body:
Infrastructure as code makes deployments repeatable.
- **ARM template (JSON):** sections $schema, contentVersion, parameters, variables, resources, outputs (functions and user-defined functions optional).
- **Bicep:** a simpler language that compiles to ARM JSON.
- Deployment scopes: resource group, subscription, management group, tenant.
- **Deployment modes:** **Incremental** (default — adds/updates, leaves other resources) vs **Complete** (deletes resources in the resource group not in the template).
- Export a template from an existing resource group or a past deployment; deploy with portal, CLI (az deployment group create), or PowerShell.

steps.title: Worked example: a minimal Bicep storage account
Try this
steps.body: Deploy a small Linux VM with no public IP, connect through Bastion, resize it, then stop (deallocate) it and check billing behaviour in Cost Management the next day.

a.text: You are Vikram. The web tier must survive the failure of an entire data centre in Central India. Which design?

choices.label: VMs across availability zones behind a Standard Load Balancer
Two VMs in an availability set
choices.feedback: An availability set protects within a data centre, not against losing it.

b.text: Traffic triples in December. You want instances added automatically based on CPU. Use…

choices.label: A Virtual Machine Scale Set with autoscale rules
choices.feedback: Yes — scale out and in automatically.

choices.label: Resize each VM to a bigger size manually
choices.feedback: Vertical scaling needs restarts and doesn't react automatically.

c.text: A cooling failure takes one data centre offline; both VMs are in it. The site goes down.

c2.text: Each resize restarts a VM during peak hours.

choices.label: Move to a scale set with autoscale

d.text: Zone-redundant scale set behind a Standard Load Balancer, defined in Bicep, deployed in Incremental mode through a pipeline. Resilient and repeatable.

quiz.q: Maximum number of fault domains in an availability set (typical)?
quiz.why: An availability set spreads VMs across up to 3 fault domains (typical), which are like separate racks with their own power and network.

quiz.q: You shut down a VM from inside Windows. Is compute still billed?
quiz.why: Shutting down from inside Windows leaves the VM allocated, so compute is still billed. You must stop (deallocate) it from Azure to stop compute charges.

quiz.q: A template deployment in Complete mode will…
options: Delete resources in the resource group not defined in the template
quiz.why: In Complete mode, Azure Resource Manager deletes resources in the resource group that are not defined in the template. Incremental mode only adds or updates, so be careful with Complete.

quiz.q: Resizing fails because the size isn't available on the current cluster. Next step?
quiz.why: If a size isn't available on the current hardware cluster, deallocate the VM first and then resize. This lets Azure place it on a cluster that supports the new size.

quiz.q: RDP to VMs without public IPs, through the browser. Use…
quiz.why: Azure Bastion gives secure RDP or SSH to VMs through the browser, over TLS, without public IPs on the VMs.

story.title: Zero-downtime releases for an exam-results site

scenes.text: A state education board's results website crashed every year on results day, and each release needed a late-night outage.
Engineer Lakshmi moved it to App Service on a Premium plan with autoscale, and used a staging slot: deploy, warm up, test, then swap into production in seconds.
A background PDF-generation service went into Azure Container Apps, scaling with the queue length.

steps.title: App Service plans
steps.body:
An **App Service plan** defines the region, the OS, and the compute (tier and instance size) that apps in it share. Tiers: Free, Shared, Basic, Standard, Premium, Isolated.
- **Scale up:** move to a bigger tier/size (more CPU, memory, features).
- **Scale out:** more instances — manual or **autoscale** (Standard tier and above).
- **Deployment slots** (Standard and above): staging, testing etc. **Swap** a warmed-up slot into production; swap back to roll back. Some settings can be marked **slot-specific** (sticky) so they don't move during swaps (e.g. a staging database connection string).
- Other features: custom domains and TLS certificates, backups, VNet integration for outbound access to private resources, private endpoints for inbound private access, authentication (Easy Auth).

steps.title: Container services
steps.body:
- **Azure Container Registry (ACR):** private registry for images (Basic, Standard, Premium; Premium adds geo-replication and private link). Build images in the cloud with ACR Tasks.
- **Azure Container Instances (ACI):** run a single container or container group quickly, billed per second; no orchestration.
- **Azure Container Apps:** serverless containers with autoscaling (including to zero) based on HTTP traffic, events or queues; revisions and traffic splitting.
- **AKS:** managed Kubernetes for full control over complex microservice platforms (see the DevOps course).

steps.title: Worked example: a slot swap with sticky settings
steps.body:
- Production slot: setting DB_CONN = prod-db (marked as deployment-slot setting).
- Staging slot: DB_CONN = staging-db (also slot setting).
- Deploy v2 to staging; test against staging-db.
- Swap: the v2 code moves to production; DB_CONN stays with each slot, so production v2 uses prod-db. If v2 misbehaves, swap again to roll back to v1.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Trying to add slots or autoscale on Basic — not available.
- Forgetting that all apps in a plan share its instances — a noisy app slows the others.
- Pulling from ACR without permission: grant the AcrPull role to the managed identity of the app/cluster.
- Assuming ACI is for long-running, auto-scaled production microservices — consider Container Apps or AKS.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Create a Standard App Service plan, deploy a sample app, add a staging slot, change a page, swap, and then swap back. Mark one setting as a slot setting and observe it stay put.

activity.prompt: Match the need to the service or feature.
pairs: Test a release, then switch it into production in seconds
Run one container for a short batch job, billed per second
Serverless containers that scale with queue length, even to zero
Full Kubernetes control for many microservices

quiz.q: Minimum App Service tier for deployment slots?
quiz.why: Deployment slots need the Standard App Service tier or higher. Free, Shared and Basic do not support them.

quiz.q: Scaling out an App Service plan means…
quiz.why: Scaling out means adding more instances of the plan. Scaling up means a bigger instance size.

quiz.q: A connection string must stay with the staging slot during swaps. Mark it as…
quiz.why: Mark a setting as a deployment slot setting (sticky) so it stays with the slot and is not swapped with the app.

quiz.q: An App Service app must pull images from ACR without passwords. Grant its managed identity…
quiz.why: AcrPull is the Azure Container Registry role that allows pulling images. Give it to the app's managed identity, so no password is needed.
All apps in an App Service plan share the plan's compute instances. The plan defines the VMs, region and size.

lessons.title: Virtual networks, NSGs, peering and routing

story.title: The database that could be reached from the internet

scenes.text: A security scan flagged that a health-tech company's database VM in Bengaluru accepted connections from any internet address on port 1433.
Network admin Ayesha redesigned the VNet: web, app and data subnets; NSGs allowing only web → app → data; no public IPs on app or data VMs.
A shared-services VNet (DNS, firewall) was peered with the app VNet. When a third VNet couldn't reach the second, she remembered: peering is not transitive.

steps.title: VNets and subnets
steps.body:
- A **VNet** has one or more address spaces (private ranges such as 10.0.0.0/16). Subnets divide it (10.0.1.0/24).
- Azure **reserves 5 IP addresses in every subnet**: the network address, the default gateway (.1), two for Azure DNS mapping (.2, .3), and the broadcast address (last). A /24 therefore has 256 − 5 = **251** usable addresses; /29 is the smallest supported IPv4 subnet (3 usable).
- Special subnets: **GatewaySubnet** (VPN/ExpressRoute gateways), **AzureBastionSubnet** (/26 or larger), **AzureFirewallSubnet**.
- Address spaces of VNets you plan to connect (peering, VPN) must **not overlap**.
- Public IP SKUs: use **Standard** (secure by default, zone-capable).

steps.title: Network security groups (NSGs) and ASGs
steps.body:
- An **NSG** contains rules: priority (100–4096; **lower number = evaluated first**), source, destination, port, protocol, Allow/Deny. The first matching rule wins.
- Default rules (priority 65000+) allow traffic within the VNet and from the Azure load balancer, and deny all other inbound; outbound to the internet is allowed by default.
- Associate NSGs with **subnets** and/or **NICs**. For inbound traffic the subnet NSG is evaluated first, then the NIC NSG; for outbound, NIC then subnet. Traffic must be allowed by both.
- **Application security groups (ASGs)** let you write rules using names such as 'asg-web' instead of IP addresses.
- Use **Effective security rules** and Network Watcher **IP flow verify** to troubleshoot.

steps.title: Peering and routing
steps.body:
- **VNet peering** (regional or global) connects VNets over Microsoft's backbone with low latency. **Not transitive:** if A↔B and B↔C, A cannot reach C unless A↔C are peered or traffic is routed through a network virtual appliance/firewall in B.
- **Gateway transit:** a peered VNet can use the hub's VPN gateway ('Allow gateway transit' on the hub, 'Use remote gateways' on the spoke).
- **User-defined routes (UDRs):** route tables override system routes — e.g. send 0.0.0.0/0 to a firewall (next hop type **Virtual appliance**). Other next hop types: Virtual network gateway, Virtual network, Internet, None.
- **Hub-and-spoke** topology: shared services in the hub; spokes peered to it.

steps.title: Worked example: rule evaluation
steps.body:
Inbound NSG on the data subnet:
- 100: Allow TCP 1433 from asg-app
- 200: Deny TCP 1433 from Any
- 65000+: defaults
A packet from an app VM (member of asg-app) on 1433 → matches rule 100 → **allowed** (rule 200 never checked).
A packet from the web subnet on 1433 → not in asg-app → rule 200 → **denied**.
If someone adds '150: Allow Any 1433 from Internet', traffic from the internet is allowed — because 150 is evaluated before 200. Order matters.

steps.title: Private access to PaaS
steps.body:
- **Service endpoints:** extend the subnet identity to a PaaS service over the backbone; the service keeps its public endpoint but can restrict access to that subnet.
- **Private endpoints (Private Link):** a NIC with a private IP in your subnet for a specific resource; combine with **private DNS zones** (e.g. privatelink.blob.core.windows.net) linked to the VNet; public access can be disabled.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Calculate usable addresses for /26, /27 and /28 subnets in Azure. (Answers: 64−5 = 59, 32−5 = 27, 16−5 = 11.)

activity.prompt: How many usable IP addresses does Azure give you in a /25 subnet?

quiz.q: NSG rules with priorities 300 (Deny) and 200 (Allow) both match. Result?
quiz.why: NSG rules are evaluated in order of priority number, with the lowest number first. The Allow at 200 is processed before the Deny at 300, so traffic is allowed.

quiz.q: VNet A is peered with B, and B with C. Can A reach C by default?
quiz.why: VNet peering is not transitive. A can't reach C through B by default; you'd need a direct A–C peering or a routing appliance in B.

quiz.q: Name of the subnet required for a VPN gateway?
quiz.why: A VPN gateway needs a dedicated subnet that is named exactly GatewaySubnet.

quiz.q: Send all internet-bound traffic through a firewall. Use…
options: User-defined route with next hop Virtual appliance
quiz.why: A user-defined route (UDR) with 0.0.0.0/0 and next hop type 'Virtual appliance', pointing to the firewall's IP, forces internet-bound traffic through the firewall.

quiz.q: Peering fails to create. Most common cause?
quiz.why: VNet peering requires non-overlapping address spaces. Overlapping ranges are the most common cause of peering failures.

lessons.title: Load balancing, DNS and hybrid connectivity

story.title: One URL, many servers, two offices

scenes.text: An e-commerce firm in Mumbai needed /images traffic to go to one pool of servers and /checkout to another, with protection from web attacks.
Network architect Rohit chose Application Gateway with WAF for path-based routing, and a Standard Load Balancer for the internal app tier.
The Delhi warehouse connected via site-to-site VPN; head office, with heavy, steady traffic, used ExpressRoute. Private DNS zones let VMs find each other by name.

steps.title: Choosing a traffic service
steps.body:
- **Azure Load Balancer (layer 4, TCP/UDP):** public or internal; distributes by a hash of source/destination IP and ports; **health probes**; load-balancing rules and inbound NAT rules. Use the **Standard** SKU (zone-redundant, secure by default, SLA).
- **Application Gateway (layer 7, HTTP/HTTPS) — regional:** URL path-based and multi-site routing, TLS termination, cookie-based session affinity, autoscaling, optional **Web Application Firewall (WAF)**.
- **Azure Front Door (layer 7) — global:** edge entry point, global HTTP load balancing, caching, WAF.
- **Traffic Manager — DNS-based global routing:** priority, weighted, performance, geographic routing methods; it does not proxy traffic.
Rule of thumb: regional + non-HTTP → Load Balancer; regional + HTTP features → Application Gateway; global HTTP → Front Door; global DNS steering of any protocol → Traffic Manager.

steps.title: Azure DNS
steps.body:
- **Public DNS zones:** host your domain's records (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, etc.) on Azure name servers; delegate the domain at your registrar by updating NS records.
- **Private DNS zones:** name resolution inside VNets; link the zone to VNets, optionally with **auto-registration** so VM records are created automatically.
- VNets can use Azure-provided DNS or custom DNS servers.

steps.title: Hybrid connectivity
steps.body:
- **Site-to-site VPN:** IPsec/IKE tunnel from an on-premises VPN device to an Azure VPN gateway, over the internet. Needs the GatewaySubnet, a local network gateway (on-premises public IP and address ranges) and a connection.
- **Point-to-site VPN:** individual devices connect (e.g. a remote admin's laptop).
- **VNet-to-VNet:** VPN between VNets (peering is usually simpler).
- **ExpressRoute:** private connection through a connectivity provider; predictable performance; does not traverse the public internet (encryption is still your choice, e.g. MACsec or IPsec over it). A VPN can serve as a backup path.
- **Azure Virtual WAN:** a managed hub for large branch networks.

steps.title: Worked example: health probes
steps.body:
An internal Standard Load Balancer has a backend pool of 3 app VMs, a health probe on HTTP /health port 8080 every 5 seconds, and a rule TCP 443 → 8443.
If VM2's app crashes, /health fails, the probe marks VM2 unhealthy and new flows go only to VM1 and VM3. When VM2 recovers, it rejoins automatically. Common outage cause: the NSG blocks the probe source — allow the AzureLoadBalancer service tag.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Using Load Balancer when you need URL path routing or WAF (needs Application Gateway / Front Door).
- Forgetting to update the registrar's NS records after creating a public zone.
- Overlapping on-premises and VNet address ranges, which breaks VPN routing.
- Assuming Traffic Manager sees HTTP paths — it only answers DNS queries.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For each, pick the service: (1) global website with caching and WAF; (2) internal SQL Always On listener; (3) /api and /images to different pools in one region; (4) failover between two regions for a non-HTTP game server. (Answers: Front Door, internal Load Balancer, Application Gateway, Traffic Manager.)

activity.prompt: Which traffic service fits?

items.text: Regional TCP load balancing for a game server
Route /checkout and /images to different backends in one region with WAF
Global HTTP entry point with edge caching
Internal load balancing for an app tier
TLS termination and cookie-based affinity for a regional web app

quiz.q: Which service supports URL path-based routing within a region?
quiz.why: Application Gateway is a regional layer-7 load balancer that supports URL path-based routing. Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4.
Traffic Manager is DNS-based: it answers DNS queries with the endpoint chosen by the routing method. It does not proxy traffic.

quiz.q: VMs in a VNet should get DNS records automatically in a private zone. Enable…
options: Auto-registration on the virtual network link
quiz.why: Auto-registration on the virtual network link in a private DNS zone creates and removes DNS records for the VMs in that VNet automatically.

quiz.q: Which hybrid option avoids the public internet?
quiz.why: ExpressRoute is a private connection through a provider and avoids the public internet. Site-to-site and point-to-site VPNs use the internet.

quiz.q: All backend VMs show unhealthy, but apps run fine. Likely cause?
quiz.why: If every backend VM shows unhealthy while the apps run fine, an NSG may be blocking the health probe. Allow the AzureLoadBalancer service tag on the probe port.

scenes.text: A clinic chain in Kerala found its file server encrypted by ransomware on a Sunday morning.

Thankfully, administrator Thomas had Azure Backup for the VMs with daily backups, soft delete and multi-user authorisation for critical operations. The attackers' attempt to delete backups was blocked.
He restored the VM from Friday night's recovery point within hours. Afterwards he added alerts for unusual sign-ins, CPU spikes and backup failures, all sent to an on-call action group.

steps.title: Azure Monitor building blocks
steps.body:
- **Metrics:** numeric time series (CPU %, disk IOPS), near real time, retained for a limited period by default.
- **Logs:** records stored in a **Log Analytics workspace**, queried with **KQL** (Kusto Query Language).
- **Activity log:** subscription-level 'who did what and when' for control-plane operations.
- **Diagnostic settings:** send resource logs and metrics to Log Analytics, a storage account or Event Hubs.
- **Azure Monitor Agent** with **data collection rules** collects guest OS logs and performance data from VMs.
- **Insights:** VM insights, Container insights, Network insights; **Application Insights** for app telemetry.

steps.title: Worked example: KQL queries
steps.body:
Which VMs stopped sending heartbeats in the last 15 minutes?
Heartbeat
| summarize LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
| where LastSeen < ago(15m)

Top 5 VMs by average CPU in the last hour:
Perf
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) and ObjectName == 'Processor' and CounterName == '% Processor Time'
| summarize AvgCPU = avg(CounterValue) by Computer
| top 5 by AvgCPU desc

(Table names depend on what you collect; newer agents may send performance data to InsightsMetrics or other tables.)

steps.title: Alerts and action groups
steps.body:
- **Alert rule** = scope (resource) + condition (metric, log search, or activity log signal) + **action group**.
- **Action groups:** who/what to notify — email, SMS, push, voice — and automation: webhook, Logic App, Azure Function, Automation runbook, ITSM.
- **Alert processing rules:** suppress notifications during planned maintenance or add action groups at scale.
- Severity levels 0 (critical) to 4 (verbose). Design alerts that are actionable — too many alerts train people to ignore them.

steps.title: Azure Backup and Site Recovery
steps.body:
- **Recovery Services vault:** backup of Azure VMs, SQL Server/SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Files, and on-premises files via the MARS agent; also hosts **Azure Site Recovery**.
- **Backup vault:** newer workloads such as Azure Blobs, Azure Disks and Azure Database for PostgreSQL.
- For Azure VM backup, the vault must be in the **same region** as the VM.
- **Backup policy:** schedule (daily/weekly or more frequent options for some workloads) and retention (daily, weekly, monthly, yearly).
- **Soft delete** keeps deleted backup data for a retention period (14 days by default) — vital against ransomware; plus **immutable vaults** and **multi-user authorisation**.
- Restore options for VMs: create a new VM, restore disks, replace existing disks, or file-level recovery.
- **Cross Region Restore** is available when the vault uses geo-redundant storage.
- **Azure Site Recovery (ASR):** continuous replication of VMs to another region for **disaster recovery**; run test failovers without affecting production. Backup = recover data to a point in time; Site Recovery = keep the business running elsewhere (low RPO/RTO).

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Creating the vault in a different region from the VMs.
- Never testing restores — a backup you haven't restored is a hope, not a plan.
- A vault can't be deleted while it still contains protected items or soft-deleted backup data.
- Confusing the activity log (control-plane operations) with guest OS logs.
- Alerting only by email to one person who is on leave — use action groups with on-call rotations.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Back up a test VM, delete a file inside it, then use file-level recovery to get it back. Create a metric alert for CPU > 80% for 5 minutes with an action group that emails you, and trigger it with a stress tool.

a.text: You are Thomas. You must back up VMs in South India. Where do you create the Recovery Services vault?

choices.label: In South India, the same region as the VMs
choices.feedback: Correct — Azure VM backup needs the vault in the same region.

choices.label: In Central India for safety
choices.feedback: For VM backup, the vault must be in the VM's region. Use GRS/Cross Region Restore for geo-protection.

b.text: An attacker with stolen admin credentials tries to delete backups. Which features help most?

choices.label: Soft delete, immutable vault and multi-user authorisation

c.text: The VMs don't appear as backup items in the other region's vault.

choices.label: Create the vault in South India

c2.text: Without protection, the attacker could have removed recovery points.

choices.label: Enable soft delete, immutability and MUA
choices.feedback: Now deletion needs extra approval and is recoverable.

d.text: Backups protected, restores tested monthly, alerts routed to an on-call action group, and Site Recovery replicating critical VMs to another region. Ready for a bad Sunday.

quiz.why: Log Analytics is queried with KQL (Kusto Query Language).

quiz.q: Who deleted a VM yesterday? Check the…
quiz.why: Control-plane operations such as deleting a VM are recorded in the Activity log. It shows who did it and when.

quiz.q: An alert must send an SMS and run a runbook. Configure…
quiz.why: An action group defines the notifications (such as SMS) and actions (such as running a runbook) that an alert triggers.

quiz.q: Default soft-delete retention for Azure Backup data (typical)?
quiz.why: Azure Backup soft delete keeps deleted backup data for 14 days by default, so it can be recovered.

quiz.q: Keep a business app running in another region if the primary region fails, with minimal data loss. Use…
quiz.why: Azure Site Recovery replicates workloads to another region for disaster recovery, so the app can fail over with minimal data loss. Backup alone restores data but does not give quick failover.

questions.q: Which load balancer works at layer 4?
questions.why: Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP). Application Gateway and Front Door work at layer 7.

questions.q: Which vault type backs up Azure VMs?
questions.why: A Recovery Services vault stores Azure VM backups and recovery points. A Key Vault is for secrets.

questions.q: How many IPs does Azure reserve in each subnet?
questions.why: Azure reserves 5 IP addresses in each subnet: the network address, broadcast address, and three for Azure services (gateway and DNS).

questions.q: Lower NSG priority numbers are evaluated…
questions.why: Lower NSG priority numbers are evaluated first, so priority 100 is checked before 4096.

questions.q: Which feature lets you test a new web app version and swap it into production?
questions.why: Deployment slots let you deploy and test a new version in a staging slot, then swap it into production.

questions.q: Scenario: two VMs must be protected against rack-level hardware failure and planned maintenance in one data centre at low cost. Use…
questions.why: An availability set spreads VMs over fault domains and update domains inside one data centre. It protects against rack failure and planned maintenance at low cost. Availability zones protect against whole data-centre failure.

questions.q: Scenario: a /27 subnet — how many VMs can get private IPs?
questions.why: A /27 has 32 addresses. Azure reserves 5, so 32 − 5 = 27 are usable for VMs.

questions.q: Scenario: spoke VNets must use the hub's VPN gateway to reach on-premises. Configure…
options: Gateway transit on the hub peering and 'use remote gateways' on spokes
A public IP on each VM
questions.why: For spokes to use the hub's VPN gateway, allow gateway transit on the hub side of the peering and enable 'use remote gateways' on the spokes' peerings.

questions.q: Scenario: an App Service on the Basic tier needs autoscale. What must you do?
options: Scale up the plan to Standard or higher
questions.why: Autoscale needs the Standard tier or higher. Basic only supports manual scaling, so scale up the plan first.

questions.q: Scenario: inbound NSG on subnet allows TCP 443; NIC NSG has no rule for 443 (only defaults). Is internet traffic on 443 allowed to the VM?
options: No — the NIC NSG's default DenyAllInBound blocks it
questions.why: Traffic must be allowed by both NSGs (the subnet and the NIC). The NIC NSG has no allow for 443, so its default DenyAllInBound blocks it.

questions.q: Scenario: a deployment in Complete mode removed a storage account. Why?
options: It was in the resource group but not in the template
questions.why: In Complete mode, resources in the resource group that are not in the template are deleted. The storage account was in the group but missing from the template.

questions.q: Scenario: VNets A (10.1.0.0/16) and B (10.1.0.0/24) cannot be peered. Fix?
options: Re-address one VNet so ranges do not overlap
questions.why: 10.1.0.0/24 lies inside 10.1.0.0/16, so the address spaces overlap and peering is blocked. Re-address one VNet so the ranges don't overlap.

questions.q: Scenario: you need a query of VMs that have not sent a heartbeat for 15 minutes, with an alert. Use…
options: Log search alert using a KQL query on the Heartbeat table
questions.why: A log search alert uses a KQL query on the Heartbeat table to find VMs with no heartbeat in 15 minutes. A CPU metric alert or an activity log alert doesn't check this.

questions.q: Scenario: a storage account must be reachable only privately from a VNet with no public access, and names must resolve correctly. Configure…
options: Private endpoint + private DNS zone linked to the VNet + disable public network access
questions.why: For private-only access, use a private endpoint, a private DNS zone linked to the VNet so the name resolves to the private IP, and disable public network access. A service endpoint alone does not give a private IP.

questions.q: Scenario: VM backups must be restorable in the paired region if the primary region is unavailable. Configure…
options: GRS vault with Cross Region Restore enabled
A second vault in the same region
questions.why: Cross Region Restore lets you restore backups in the paired region. It needs a geo-redundant (GRS) vault with the feature enabled.

courses.title: Beyond admin: Azure developer (AZ-204) and Azure AI engineer (AI-102) overview
courses.summary: A map of what developers and AI engineers build on Azure: compute and storage for apps, security with managed identities and Key Vault, messaging and APIs, monitoring — and Azure AI services, Azure OpenAI, AI Search and responsible AI. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can describe the main service areas a developer exam typically covers and pick services for a scenario
Learners can choose between Event Grid, Event Hubs, Service Bus and Queue Storage
Learners can secure apps with managed identities and Key Vault
Learners can map AI scenarios to Azure AI services, Azure OpenAI and AI Search and plan hands-on study

lessons.title: Developer path: building apps on Azure

story.title: An order pipeline for a D2C brand

scenes.text: A skincare brand in Bengaluru was growing fast. Every order needed payment confirmation, an invoice PDF, warehouse notification and an SMS.
Developer Arnav built it on Azure: an App Service API, an Azure Function triggered by new orders, Service Bus queues between steps, Cosmos DB for orders, Blob Storage for invoices.
No passwords lived in code: each component used a managed identity, and secrets that had to exist lived in Key Vault.

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline. Exam codes, outlines and even whole exams change or are retired over time — check the official exam page before you plan your study.

steps.title: Compute for developers
steps.body:
- **App Service:** web apps and APIs; deployment slots, autoscale, settings, logging.
- **Azure Functions:** event-driven code. A function has exactly one **trigger** (HTTP, timer, queue, blob, Event Grid, Service Bus, Cosmos DB…) and optional input/output **bindings** that connect to data without boilerplate. Hosting options include consumption-style serverless plans and dedicated/premium plans; durable functions orchestrate long workflows.
- **Containers:** build and push images to Azure Container Registry; run on Container Apps or Container Instances.

steps.title: Storage and data for apps
steps.body:
- **Blob Storage** via SDKs: containers, blobs, metadata, access tiers, lifecycle.
- **Azure Cosmos DB:** globally distributed NoSQL database; choose a **partition key** with high cardinality and even access; five consistency levels from strong to eventual (strong, bounded staleness, session, consistent prefix, eventual); throughput measured in request units (RUs); change feed for event-driven processing.

steps.title: Security for developers
steps.body:
- **Microsoft identity platform / MSAL:** sign users in and get tokens (OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect).
- **Managed identities:** system-assigned (tied to one resource's lifecycle) or user-assigned (standalone, shareable) identities that let code get tokens for Azure services without secrets.
- **Azure Key Vault:** store secrets, keys and certificates; access via RBAC; soft delete and purge protection.
